> ah sorry, i didnt see the zulip link.

Yea I keep trying to find the MVP slice here, but the scope that would be seemingly acceptable to that keeps expanding, but there are two sides to it.

One one hand, if we can get the syntax side down, then the backend can be built piecemeal over time.

I.E. if `align(EXPR)` was acceptable, or if the language side can be established at any level, then the backend can evolve slowly and attribute refactors can be done as needed rather than all at once.

That was the original intention of my PR. Defend the semantics, shim the backend towards an eventual refactor. 

There's multiple routes to the same endgame here, so this issue is meant to service the larger discussion, but I wanted to lay out my intentions here.

author: tmandry

body:
This looks great to me, and I'd love to see the ability to set alignment using const expressions.

The alternative approach in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/154730 is interesting, but seems like it'll need substantial additional design to address usability (e.g. having to handle the `Align` field in initialization and pattern matching, and having it show up in `derive(Debug)`, much like `PhantomData`).

I think it's important that we work towards usability of the alignment mechanism we have, `repr(align(...))`. And making const paths, and ideally const expressions, work in that would be a huge improvement that I've regularly seen people request. (That would allow factoring out common alignments, for instance.)

author: mejrs

body:
Great input, all.

Should I create a new PR or rework the existing? Either's fine.

I see two options that satisfy the concerns and opinions put forward. Both options share the same backend: a new `ast::Repr` AST node with `AnonConst` payloads, lowered through the normal AST → HIR → MIR pipeline, modeled on `#[define_opaque]`.

They differ only in the surface vehicle:

**Option 1 (@petrochenkov's first preference):** Migrate `#[repr]` to a built-in proc macro across an edition. Cleanest semantically; probably needs edition coordination as stated. 

**Option 2 (his second listed option):** Active built-in attribute materialized in `rustc_expand`, same model as `cfg`/`cfg_attr`. Surface stays `#[repr(align(CONST))]`. One behavioral change (validation moves to parse time, including inside `cfg(FALSE)` — flagged in RFC #3659, worth a crater run).

cc @joshtriplett @tmandry @programmerjake for the directly related input they gave.

I've done some testing with the above to good success, about ready to clean it up if it is desired. Or if anyone else has a criticism to be explored, I think I like option 1 better as it will open the door for any other attributes that may be desired in this process later.

Both options defend the existing attribute syntax.
author: BarronKane

body:
I'm not exactly sure how it works, but I'm worried a proc-macro or something similar will end up removing the `#[repr(...)]` in later macro inputs, which would be a breaking change, e.g.:
```rust
#[repr(align(128)]
#[derive(MyTrait)]
pub struct S;
```

the `#[derive(MyTrait)]` needs to be able to see the `#[repr(...)]` on the struct definition (I'm assuming that's what currently happens but haven't verified), but if it's a proc-macro I expect the attribute will get removed before the derives run.

body:
The reason for the nonsensical assembly is that the generated MIR has unconditional UB, it's not an issue with codegen:

* `std::mem::transmute` lowers to `CastKind::Transmute` at the `LowerIntrinsics` Mir pass
* `CastKind::Transmute` where the src and dest have differing sizes is well-formed MIR but UB to execute
* `CastKind::Transmute` where the src and dest have differing sizes is lowered as `bx.unreachable_nonterminator()` ([src](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/main/compiler/rustc_codegen_ssa/src/mir/rvalue.rs#L223))
* `rustc_codegen_llvm`'s [`unreachable_nonterminator`](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/main/compiler/rustc_codegen_ssa/src/traits/builder.rs#L141) emits `store i1 true, ptr poison, align 1` which is LLVM's "the preferred LLVM incantation" for non-basic-block-terminator `unreachable`
* `store i1 true, ptr poison` naturally lowers to `movb [rax], 1` without optimizations

body:
Yes, this is #149484 working as intended (from my point of view :-)).

The later errors are suppressed because the first error inside the diesel macro suggests that the missing symbols in that module are likely caused by the macro failure. We want the user to focus on the root cause.

You're right that in this specific case, the later errors are not actually caused by the macro expansion error. So it is not ideal that we don't report all the errors here.

In my opinion, making the root cause more visible and hiding the fallout from the macro error is worth showing fewer errors on the first pass (at least for a human user, maybe for a test suite or an AI agent, the trade-off might go the other way.)

I'll defer to the rust team if they think the change should be reverted.
author: ogoffart

body:
We discussed this diagnostics change during [compiler triage meeting today](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/238009-t-compiler.2Fmeetings/topic/.5Bweekly.5D.202026-04-23/near/590484734). From team members present during the triage meeting, the thought was:

* The original motivation in #149484 makes sense to help pinpoint the "initial" points of failure, instead of having it drown in a sea of other additional errors. Generally, the tradeoff consideration is that it's better to show less (but the most important) errors instead of reporting all possible errors. However, at times this will unfortunately suppress too many, including genuine ones.
* We want to wait a bit (maybe a release cycle or two) to hear more feedback / examples about this diagnostics change. There were a number of users in the original issue #68838 (that the PR fixed) asking for this behavior so at least some people find it helpful.
  * This is diagnostics only so there's no stability guarantees, we can walk this back based on more feedback if needed.
  * Perhaps it could be tuned, though it's not quite clear in what ways at this moment.
* At this time we don't think a revert is warranted.

We'll tag this as P-medium.

`MetadataBlob::new` checks for truncated metadata. It does not do a through check for errors. That would be way too expensive. Crashing on invalid crate metadata is the intended failure mode. It means either you are intentionally mucking with the crate metadata, you have a hardware failure or there is a bug somewhere in rustc or your filesystem. Rustc is not a web service that needs to keep running even when you intentionally try to crash it.

body: The error is telling you that `Self: 'b` is not satisfied (Since `Self = &'c u8`). It marks `Self::Y<'b>` because `Self` must live for at least `'b` to be able to pass `'b` as an argument, per the declaration of `Y`.
author: maxdexh
taylordotfish

body:
It's somewhat an issue with implied bounds.  `get_y` has to be callable for all lifetimes because the `where Self: 'a` bound is not implied.  But `Y<'a>` is only defined when `Self: 'a`.

If you add the bound to the method and implementation, it compiles (with the same function signatures).

In the op, `x_to_y` has an implied `Self::X: 'b` bound, but this is not sufficient to conclude `Self: 'b`, so `Y<'b>` may still be not defined. If you change the bound on `Y<'a>` to `where Self::X: 'a`, the implementation compiles with the same signature. 

In summary things work smoother when the bounds on the GAT and method line up (via explicit bounds or implied bounds).

It's not clear from the OP if you actually need `Self: 'a` in the unminimized code.

https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=6a37ecaade8abed8412c50db02b92550

> Intuitively, I feel like when I implement a trait, I should be able to use the same function signatures that appear in the trait definition.

I agree that would be ideal.  I don't know how achievable it is.  There are some other exceptions beyond those in this issue too.

body: @RalfJung Does rustc have two different notions of subtyping? `Thing<F1>` and `Thing<F2>` cannot be coerced to each other in surface rust, so presumably they aren't subtypes of each other. But you seem to be saying that these two types are subtypes of each other.
author: theemathas

body:
> I'll make https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/155512 add a similar assertion to codegen.

Turns out that would still not trigger the ICE during codegen. The ICE occurs because Miri optimistically checks `mir_assign_valid_types` for every transmute so that it can do a more efficient assignment if the two sides of the transmute end up actually being compatible types (so a failure of that check just leads to a less efficient codepath, not an ICE). However as part of that check we also do check that if the two types do happen to be considered subtypes, they have the same layout, and that check fails.

> Does rustc have two different notions of subtyping? Thing<F1> and Thing<F2> cannot be coerced to each other in surface rust, so presumably they aren't subtypes of each other. But you seem to be saying that these two types are subtypes of each other.

I have no idea. `relate_types` and the things it calls are black boxes to me.^^

body:
I think this is a bug in `util::relate_types` where it's not checking region constraints between higher ranked stuff so is incorrectly considering the two types to have a subtyping relation when they actually do not. This should get fixed when we start handling lifetime constraints involving placeholders eagerly (https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/assumptions_on_binders.html)

I'm not sure what a good short term fix would be
author: BoxyUwU

body:
Ah... yeah that would explain this. Also after reading its code quite a few times I didn't realize `relate_types` would just entirely ignore all lifetime constraints. Those APIs seem quite tricky to use correctly.

Many uses of `relate_types` are just checking that MIR is valid, so an incorrect `true` answer is not unsound (but could hide other bugs). However the way the interpreter uses this actually relies on `true` answers being correct... we should probably stop doing that then.

oh, I see what's happening.
the lint sees a `OptionLikeEnum<NonNullType>`, and so it assumes that the enum and its inner type have the same size.
...but I guess that "Not having a separate discriminant" and "having the same size as the inner type" are not the same thing.

I... somehow have not thought about this `#[repr(align(N))]` thing when working on that lint, sorry about that. (I didn't even know it existed, I'll have to look its semantics up)
Is `I want this alignment` something you can even do in C?

... in any case, I see a few options right now:
- not do anything right now, and just put this consideration into the work being done on the lint
  (that PR above, which I think will need a discussion with the appropriate team because there are quite a few changes in what the lint says and doesn't say)
  (most likely the worst option, given how easy the next two are)
- bandaid fix that (for now) assumes these aligned reprs make things FFI-unsafe, and then think about it some more
- bandaid fix that just ignores this, to err on the side of false negatives when working with lints
   (easiest solution to implement, a probably-literal one-line-fix)
- determine when `repr(align(N))` is FFI-safe (eg: if it lands on the same alignment as C would want) and push this as a separate fix to the lint

body:
The issue reproduces just with `#[unsafe(export_name = "")]`, no need for the newline. 

An empty argument to `export_name` has some interesting behavior: it circumvents rust name mangling and instead has LLVM make up a symbol:

https://godbolt.org/z/555eKdjWe

I wonder if that has any practical uses, or whether we should just disallow the empty string as an argument.
author: folkertdev

body: We should disallow that. If the item is defined in a different crate than it is used, LLVM would make up entirely different symbols and you did get a linker error. Even within a crate there is no guarantee that the definition and the user end up in the same codegen unit. Basically the use case I can think of where it would not be UB is a `#[used]` static that is not referenced anywhere.
author: bjorn3

body:
Basically the use case I can think of where it would not be UB is a `#[used]` static that is not referenced anywhere.

But even in this case, is there an advantage to LLVM generating that name? You could just use `#[used]` without `export_name` or `no_mangle` for the same effect right?

> > test-float-parse really hasn't changed notably
> 
> I think we have changed some of the float parsing code more recently though, right? e.g., [2ae6c61](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/2ae6c6176e1e058368ff4035281dbce1c8f9f30b) landed pretty recently.
> 
> Or does all the num-bigint stuff not really get influenced by std's float parsing/serialization code? From a brief poke it does look like it's somewhat involved.

They should be reasonably disconnected. We parse the input once using `std` (within the `catch_unwind`), then parse again to a `BigRational` (`Rational::Parse`) then check the error between the two (`validate_real`). The `BigRational` step is done by splitting the decimal then using `BigInt::from_str`, to avoid relying relying on any float-esque parsing other than the simple `split on '.' -> compute pow -> parse int` that's there.

```
target/bpfel-unknown-none/debug/bpf-bug: ELF 64-bit LSB relocatable, eBPF, version 1 (SYSV), not stripped
```

The nightly versions you've compared use different major versions of LLVM:

```
rustc 1.95.0-nightly (e96bb7e44 2026-01-27)
[...]
LLVM version: 21.1.8
```

```
rustc 1.95.0-nightly (de6d33c03 2026-01-28)
[...]
LLVM version: 22.1.0
```

So it's very likely that you have an old bpf-linker version that's built for LLVM 21, not 22.

That said, in such situations, LLVM should include the versions in error message, making it somehow clear that the LLVM mismatch is the issue, e.g.:

```
ERROR llvm: Invalid record (Producer: 'LLVM 21.1.8' Reader: 'LLVM 22.1.2')
```

In your case, it threw only `ERROR llvm: Invalid record`, which definitely makes it harder to undestand. We already have an issue in bpf-linker proposing better error messages and LLVM bitcode version detection on our side (aya-rs/bpf-linker#319), I suggest we move the discussion there. Also, given that the error message is less understandable now, I will give it more urgency.

Ok, I've been testing mingw dlltool and I can't get it to work with paths that have spaces. The issue is the `--temp-prefix` argument. It always splits on the space no matter how I quote it. #5  0x00007ff62a143bab in std::sys::backtrace::__rust_begin_short_backtrace
()
#6  0x00007ff62a14de0f in
core::ops::function::FnOnce::call_once{{vtable.shim}} ()
#7  0x00007ff62a1baca7 in
<std::sys::thread::windows::Thread>::new::thread_start ()
#8  0x00007ffbdcece8d7 in KERNEL32!BaseThreadInitThunk ()

0x7ff62a141e1b: ret

`core::core_arch::x86::avx512vnni::_mm512_dpbusd_epi32`.

This strongly suggests that code compiled with `-C target-cpu=native` is
using AVX-512 VNNI on this machine.

The affected CPU is Intel i9-7980XE (Skylake-X), which supports AVX-512 but
not AVX-512 VNNI.

`rustc -C target-cpu=native --print cfg | grep target_feature` reports:

Note also that this
```rust
let nibbles = core::array::from_fn::<_, 16, _>(|i| { ...whatever... });
nibbles.iter().enumerate().fold(0, |acc, (i, &n)| acc | (u64::from(n) << (i * 4)))
```
trips the warning in <https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.array.html#note-on-performance-and-stack-usage> for me.

If you just want to iterate something, you're probably going to be better off *not* materializing it into an array.

I guess it'd fail without profiler if you disable LLVM download from CI.
This is not very actionable by us at this point, unless we want to make custom hacks to LLD or LLVM build system to gracefully remove sframe.

Upstream bug report: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/156667#issuecomment-3252227547

Link to discussion about related Google internal bug report: https://github.com/google/perf_data_converter/pull/194#discussion_r2830008044

I see that Debian put an effort to make users suffer by implicitly enabling sframe, but backtracked from that before Ubuntu 26.04 branching and not enabled it since: https://salsa.debian.org/toolchain-team/gcc/-/commit/bd33f862a3f93c3d3b1fbc8dfb6b0366905d7ab4. author: Kobzol

body:
Okay, I found the issue. The problem is that we populate the git info in `src/tools/cargo` *before* the Cargo submodule is initialized. Bootstrap used to unconditionally checkout the `cargo` submodule before, but this no longer happens, so we don't have Cargo populated and the git info is empty. At the same time, the source tarball step vendors dependencies, so during its execution it actually checkouts all submodules, so when you run it for the second time, the files appear there (which expains the heisenbug).

Fixing this is a bit tricky, because we unconditionally checkout all submodules on CI, so the git info file is there. But in the local reproduction instructions, we don't currently do that. We can't easily do it in bootstrap without hacks, because the git info is gathered before the source tarball step runs, so at that point checking out the Cargo submodule doesn't help.

We could just hardcode checking out Cargo in the reproduction instructions, but that's a bit hacky, because in the future another submodule could have a similar issue.

I'm tempted to solve it by just adding `--recursive` to the reproduction clone instructions. It will make the command slower, but it should simulate more closely what we do in CI, and thus make reproduction easier.

body:
The error comes from https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/597d9e43be882cdbd218e58c4f7efb2fa3da7540/library/std/src/sys/thread_local/key/unix.rs#L25-L33

On Haiku, `target_thread_local` is not enabled, so `thread_local!` falls back to an OS/pthread-key based implementation. When `pthread_key_create` fails, std aborts with `fatal runtime error: out of TLS keys`.

In 1.94.x, `parse_attribute_list` finalizes all parsers unconditionally, which touches each parser's `thread_local!` state even if that attribute was never used. Since there are early and late parser sets, sumed to more than size of 200, this can easily exceed platforms that only provide the POSIX-minimum 128 TLS keys.

There is a relevant fix: #151382. 
That fix is not in 1.94.1, but it is contained in 1.95.0. So it would be very useful to test whether Rust 1.95.0 still reproduces this on Haiku. 

If 1.95.0 works, this issue is likely fixed by #151382, or could be considered for a backport.
author: chenyukang

body:
But seems #151382 changed rustc only runs the finalizers for parsers that actually accepted an attribute. This avoids eagerly touching all parser TLS states, and should significantly reduce the number of pthread TLS keys used in normal compilations.

seems it still a mitigation of the problem. Each attribute parser still has its own potential `thread_local!` state. If a compilation actually uses enough different parsed attributes, rustc may still initialize many TLS states.

I proposed a change on Haiku side to increase the number of keys from 256 (same as FreeBSD and NetBSD) to 512 (same as OpenBSD): https://review.haiku-os.org/c/haiku/+/10976

You may still want to fix this on Rust side if you aim for strict POSIX conformance. I don't know if FreeBSD and NetBSD have issues or if they can use other TLS stoage methods to avoid this.

author: waddlesplash

body:
> You may still want to fix this on Rust side if you aim for strict POSIX conformance. I don't know if
> FreeBSD and NetBSD have issues or if they can use other TLS storage methods to avoid this.

The FreeBSD source code still has just [WRONG: 128, not 256 nor] 256, not 512. FreeBSD's 1.94.0 bootstrap fails for the "out of TLS keys" in an armv7 poudriere(-devel) jail on aarch64 that supports armv7 as well, preventing building of 1.95.0 (lang/rust port). [correction: 1.93.0's part of boostraping 1.94.0 worked, a later 1.94.0 stage got the failure].  (The FreeBSD ports infrastructure does not cross build port-packages.)

It seems one has to back up to the last working bootstrap, then update/improve all following after that to get to a working build of 1.95.0 for armv7. [It looks like 1.95.0 on/for armv7 can build based on target_thread_local use. That likely does not solve the general "out of TLS keys" problem based on what OpenBSD and Haiku found.]

I'm unsure if changing the [correction: 256] to 512 is technically an ABI change for the FreeBSD OS. [It is.] If it is, that would be a big deal to change that in the FreeBSD source code. If an ABI issue, it could not [normally] change for `14.*-RELEASE` or `15.*-RELEASE`, only main (later: `16.*-RELEASE` once it is branched). [But the 1.95.0 compiler may not need such.]

I will note that for some reason, only armv7 has the "out of TLS keys" build issue (for main, which is the context I'm familiar with). It is the only 32-bit FreeBSD OS variant for `15.*-RELEASE` and main. `14.*-RELEASE` still supports i386. lang/rust for i386 has not had any "out of TLS keys" problems for its builds, including for building 1.95.0. (I looked at the logs from the official port-package builder for 14.3-RELEASE.)

(At this time no port-package builder is active for armv7: resource limitations caused that to stop. So testing is via personal builds by various folks.)

Ahh:

```
/usr/include/limits.h:#define	_POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX	128
/usr/include/pthread.h:#define	PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX			256

        case _SC_THREAD_KEYS_MAX:
```

author: markmi

body:
This looks correct to me, _POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX is only the minimal value that POSIX requires to support. It should be unused by FreeBSD itself, but available to software. See the opengroup specification for limits.h which explains this.

As long as FreeBSD uses PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX as the actual limit, you are fine.
author: pulkomandy

body:
> This looks correct to me, _POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX is only the minimal value that POSIX requires to support. It should be unused by FreeBSD itself, but available to software. See the opengroup specification for limits.h which explains this.
> 
> As long as FreeBSD uses PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX as the actual limit, you are fine.
```
# grep -r _POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX /usr/include/ /usr/src/
/usr/include/limits.h:#define	_POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX	128
/usr/src/contrib/netbsd-tests/include/t_limits.c:#ifdef	_POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX
/usr/src/contrib/netbsd-tests/include/t_limits.c:	{ "_POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX",	_POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX,		128  },
/usr/src/usr.bin/getconf/limits.gperf:_POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX, _POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX
/usr/src/include/limits.h:#define	_POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX	128

# grep THREAD_KEYS_MAX /usr/src/usr.bin/getconf/limits.gperf
_POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX, _POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX
```
So _POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX basically does look unused.

However, OpenBSD had 256 and increased PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX to 512 because of the "out of TLS keys" failures it was getting and Haiku is still reporting more "out of TLS keys" failures than before. Just having 1.95.0 does not seem to be a full/general solution, leaving the FreeBSD potential increase to 512 still at issue to may more work.

body:
According to all currently known theory, if this form of this issue is currently affecting OpenBSD, FreeBSD and Haiku, it should also be reproducible in Android,

however, while I was able to reproduce a different form of this issue in the past in Rust 1.90 in Android,

- https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/147590

I am no longer able to reproduce it in Rust 1.96 on Android and struggle to reproduce it with any projects that I'm attempting to build.

If you'd like to help me by making reproduction steps, please test them in OpenBSD, FreeBSD or Haiku, not Android, unless you are experienced with Android app development. This is because:

- If exactly the same reproduction steps that trigger this issue on a different operating system also trigger it on Android, that would help me to understand that this issue in particular does also affect Android
- If the Rust installation for Android used is derived from Termux's, there is currently a patch in it that must be manually removed and the entire Rust installation recompiled in order to reset Termux's Rust back closer to the upstream behavior regarding this issue, in order to troubleshoot it or collect logs https://github.com/termux/termux-packages/blob/35c0033a8c4b70d8ef2c9091af8c048f7f8419d8/packages/rust/0007-use-emulated-tls-on-android.patch I have done that locally in my attempts to reproduce this issue, but the steps are tedious and not straightforward for people who are not already focused on Android.

These steps showing the issue occurring in Haiku during the original report of this form of this issue are, potentially unfortunately, not currently reproducing it for me on Android:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/lordmulder/sponge-hash-aes256.git
cd sponge-hash-aes256
cargo build --release
```

could someone confirm whether those steps still reproduce this issue for them on their operating system or not, in Rust 1.96?

To summarize clearly, I'm basically worried that the issue could still be affecting Android in unknown edge cases, but might have ceased to be reproducible with the majority of tests that could previously reproduce it.

body: We fixed the FreeBSD issue by switching back to ELF ABI TLS.  Using pthread TLS was a temporary workaround for an rtld (ld.so) bug in processing certain relocations that is now no longer needed.

body:
There is a PR to address this problem but it is having trouble motivating it because its current implementation also involves potential performance regressions for tier 1 platforms.

Any weight on the "but it makes things work" side of the scale would be useful, and would be provided by identifying specific packages that don't work when built by current 1.96.1 or next week's 1.97.0 rustc, on a specific OS version, despite working on another OS. Perhaps @chitao1234 knows one?

As a side note: We do not aim for "strict POSIX conformance" in libstd's implementation. We try to have a good implementation, and our shared "Unix" code does expect POSIX conformance as a minimum. But in practice, we rely on target maintainers to contribute their expertise in designing workarounds when platforms inevitably conform to POSIX in... creative ways.

(We don't support the "static" ELF TLS model, only the "dynamic" one, is that the problem here? -- But if rustc is compiled as a shared object, which it would be on Haiku as everything's a shared object, then presumably that's not the issue?) author: waddlesplash

body:
For that, it is very possible (I am saying this without doing the history dive to verify for sure, but based on experience of previous similar situations) that there's no really good reason and our contributors and reviewers simply weren't sure at the time of the PRs adding the target or modifying how we do thread-local storage. There could also have been a transient issue in codegen or linking that is no longer an issue. In any such a case, emulated/key-based TLS was likely seen as a "safe" fallback which makes sure things work, and then no one checked for years.

If you know that your system supports a TLS model better than the one we use, then feel free to send a PR modifying our upstream target specifications!

As a reminder, we don't run tests for tier 2 targets ourselves, but we do verify we can build them. That usually happens in a cross-build situation from Linux hosts, however, so we won't necessarily know if your rustc works on e.g. self-bootstrap with your system as host or any other TLS-stressing situations, and you may wish to verify that with a local patch first.

I wonder if we should add:

Part of the issue is that constifying iterator is a very entangled mess. Either we drop a 10k LOC PR at some point, or we try to get the basics to work (slices, ranges). We are trying the latter, but it regularly causes circular dependencies unless some hacks (using while loops instead of iterators) are used.

I don't know how to do this better, but def happy to have much stronger restrictions or even reverting some of the more hacky changes

At least from the impression I got, short of high-impact projects like constifying `Iterator`, most reviewers were hesitant to introduce more const hacks just for the sake of it and would rather only make changes that would ultimately be required in the final code.

It's been a while and not everyone has the same view on that, though, so, I think that standardising would be a good idea.

Personally, I also wanted to help out a lot for this effort but outright gave up because a lot of people were ignoring my desires to do things in a particular order and not bother reviewers constantly to Merge Now, and it was just exhausting to have to work around people in this manner. body:
> A complete unstably constified standard library isn't necessary for proving out const traits, yet many PRs seem to be aiming for this.

If I remember correctly, I have seen multiple conversations of roughly the form:
“Why isn’t <generic function> unstably const?”
“Nobody has done it yet. Send a PR.”

This suggests to me that there is an assumption in the community that const traits *are* intended to be usable-on-nightly. Therefore, if this policy is to reject constification that is purely for the sake of users of the standard library, there should be some amount of attention to getting the word out (such as any or all of a blog post, a note in the tracking issue, and a note in the unstable book) so that people aren’t given bad advice and have a disappointing contribution experience.
author: kpreid

body:
As context (and without meaning to weigh in on the proposed guidelines specifically), for my part, from a lang side, I expect that we will do const traits and that they'll have the semantics currently in nightly.  There remains some discussion over syntax (including what might be implied in bounds in a future edition).

The work to constify the standard library has been helpful for informing these design discussions: it paints a picture of what the future holds for us and what the challenges will be both here and in the ecosystem — for migration, for ergonomics, etc. — as we try to make things maximally `const`.  I appreciate the work that's gone into that.

But I understand that review bandwidth is limited.  This isn't an ask to accept things if they're too costly.
author: traviscross

body:
This seems to be a question about whether or not const traits will be stabilized soon or if the semantics will be kept. I'm not trying to speak for T-libs here, but I think if the semantics and syntax are not to change, there shouldn't be an issue with adding more const traits since we know we will stick with them.

But of course the question is whether the syntax and semantics will change. The recent [Zulip discussion](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/213817-t-lang/topic/const.20traits.20in.202026) left me quite discouraged and unsure about the path to stabilization for this feature. In the case where syntax and semantics still remain undecided, it seems good to move forward with the proposal as written.

body:
I've submitted a fix for this in #155891.
The ICE stems from the assert_ne!(location.block, successor.block) check in
ssa_range_prop::visit_terminator. This assertion fails when CFG simplification
introduces a self-loop — for example, when a loop body is collapsed into a single
basic block that branches to itself.
The PR replaces the strict assertion with an early return to skip range propagation
for self-loop successors, and adds a regression test to cover this case.

body:
The real issue is this warning from the sendfile manpage:  https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sendfile.2.html#NOTES

       If out_fd refers to a socket or pipe with zero-copy support,
       callers must ensure the transferred portions of the file referred
       to by in_fd remain unmodified until the reader on the other end of
       out_fd has consumed the transferred data.

The mailing list message clarifies that this also applies to splice, even without `SPLICE_F_MOVE` (this is what I previously misunderstood). I think this behavior is still there today since it's one of the things that makes splice fast.

std is a library used in many contexts, including socket IO (where this problem could occur) and in privileged processes (where avoiding data races is important).
I assume `cat` is less commonly used in such contexts.

body:
Looks like it's a bad interaction between CMake 4 and sccache, not sure who should fix the bug?

AI generated root cause:

### What changed

The CI runner image updated between the two builds, bringing in CMake 4.0:

| | Small log (Apr 20) | Large log (Apr 25) |
|---|---|---|
| Runner image | `20260318.50.1` | `20260419.19.1` |
| CMake version | 3.x | **4.x** |
| sccache binary | identical (~19MB) | identical (~19MB) |
| Ninja binary | identical (1.11.1) | identical (1.11.1) |
| LLVM source | identical | identical |
| sccache stats | 100% C++ cache hit | 100% C++ cache hit |

### The CMake commit

[`ed0f48e79b` — "clang-cl: use gcc depfiles over /showIncludes"](https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/-/commit/ed0f48e79bd7cffe1fcc18cc6b8539219f14f6d6) (Fixes: [#27594](https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/-/issues/27594))

This commit switches clang-cl from MSVC-style `/showIncludes` dependency tracking to gcc-style depfiles (`-clang:-MD -clang:-MT -clang:-MF`), to enable `#embed` dependency support.

### Mechanism

**Before (CMake 3.x):** CMake generated Ninja build rules with `deps = msvc`. Ninja passed `/showIncludes` to the compiler and **filtered** the resulting `Note: including file:` lines from its output (using them internally for dependency tracking).

**After (CMake 4.0):** CMake generates Ninja build rules with `deps = gcc`, using `.d` depfiles instead. Ninja no longer passes `/showIncludes` and no longer filters `Note: including file:` lines.

**The sccache interaction:** When sccache handles clang-cl compilations that have a depfile, it [internally adds `-showIncludes`](https://github.com/mozilla/sccache/blob/b81fdbb/src/compiler/msvc.rs#L969-L971) to the preprocessor command for its own dependency tracking. The resulting `Note: including file:` output is stored as part of the cached stdout. On cache hits (100% for C++ in both builds), sccache replays this stored stdout. Since Ninja is now using `deps = gcc`, it doesn't recognize these lines as dependency output and prints all of them verbatim — producing ~1.85M extra lines (~253MB) of noise.

I'm seeing the same problem when building rust for my ports system (GARStow). In my case, I'm building rust 1.95.0 from the source tarball unpacked in `/src/rust/rust/work/rustc-1.95.0-src`, using my previously-packaged rust 1.94.1, with:

```
./configure --prefix=/gar --enable-extended --enable-local-rust --enable-vendor --set=llvm.download-ci-llvm=false --disable-llvm-static-stdcpp
./x.py build
DESTDIR=/some/staging/dir ./x.py install
```

After the `error: cannot update the lock file` failure message, I diffed the rust source tree against the original tarball contents, and it's not just `Cargo.lock` that's changed - it's reverted many of the source files under `compiler` to older versions too.

So I ran the whole build again under `strace -f` to see where on earth it had got the older files from... It turns out that `bootstrap` has copied them from my rust 1.94.1 installation in `/gar/packages/rust-1.94.1`, which includes a `lib/rustlib/rustc-src/rust` subdirectory containing `Cargo.lock` and the `compiler` and `library` subdirs with the source files.

In the strace log, it looks like this (with a lot of intervening lines elided):

```
8298  symlink("/src/rust/rust/work/rustc-1.95.0-src", "/src/rust/rust/work/rustc-1.95.0-src/build/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/stage0-sysroot/lib/rustlib/rustc-src/rust") = 0
8298  openat(AT_FDCWD, "/gar/packages/rust-1.94.1/lib", O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK|O_CLOEXEC|O_DIRECTORY) = 4
... a lot of tree-walking later ...
8298  unlink("/src/rust/rust/work/rustc-1.95.0-src/build/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/stage0-sysroot/lib/rustlib/rustc-src/rust/Cargo.lock") = 0
8298  openat(AT_FDCWD, "/gar/packages/rust-1.94.1/lib/rustlib/rustc-src/rust/Cargo.lock", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 8
8298  openat(AT_FDCWD, "/src/rust/rust/work/rustc-1.95.0-src/build/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/stage0-sysroot/lib/rustlib/rustc-src/rust/Cargo.lock", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC|O_CLOEXEC, 0100644) = 9
8298  copy_file_range(8, NULL, 9, NULL, 1073741824, 0) = 155159
```

So it's made a symlink `stage0-sysroot/lib/rustlib/rustc-src/rust` that points to the 1.95.0 source tree, then recursively copied 1.94.1's `lib` directory into `stage0-sysroot/lib`, overwriting `Cargo.lock` and the source files through the symlink.

I'm not familiar with how `bootstrap` works, but it looks like this matches the code in `core/build_steps/compile.rs` following the `// Link all libstd rlibs/dylibs into the sysroot location` comment - which suggests that it's not intending to copy the contents of that subdir...

If I remove `lib/rustlib/rustc-src` from my 1.94.1 installation, then nothing gets overwritten and the build seems to proceed happily.

body:
**Sharing an update**

I looked into this issue and found two separate bugs and both are most likely related to the [`annotate-snippets`](https://github.com/rust-lang/annotate-snippets-rs) crate.

`annotate-snippets` is used by the Rust compiler to format diagnostic reports. I verified that the suggestion span generated by rustc is correct and the incorrect output appears to come from how `annotate-snippets` renders that span in terminal.

I have not looked deep into the exact internal cause in `annotate-snippets` yet but I let AI do the initial investigation and it found likely causes are:


1. The final raw-string delimiter line is not rendered

   The missing line 10 appears to come from `annotate-snippets`’ diff renderer. It has duplicate-last-line elision logic, and in this case the multiline deletion starts mid-line and ends mid-line. Because the post-edit final line text matches the original final line text, the renderer incorrectly elides the final removed raw-string delimiter line.

2. The red removal color is not applied consistently

   This also appears to be in `annotate-snippets`’ diff renderer. Removed diff lines are initially printed with only the `-` marker styled as removal/red, while the removed source text is printed unstyled. A later pass then tries to apply the removal style over computed deleted ranges.

   For this multiline raw-string deletion, that row/range calculation does not cover all removed source text correctly, so only parts of the removed lines are red and the rest remains unstyled.

_(The above findings is generated by AI and I have not verified it yet)_

Tomorrow, I will be verifying if the findings from AI are correct or wrong and then create a new issue on https://github.com/rust-lang/annotate-snippets-rs/issues and maybe even a PR too

body:
this is part of our general story around well-formedness checking, we don't check requirements involving bound variables right now, so we never check that `<G as Trait<'life>>::Output` is well-formed as `'life` is higher-ranked. 

This is mostly fine as instantiating this `for` will have to prove that the resulting type is well-formed, at which point we'd error if `'life` is something that is not `'a`. However, this is brittle and does actually result in unsoundnesses, e.g. #25860.

We're currently working on fixing this as part of https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-project-goals/2026/assumptions_on_binders.html

body:
Oh no, is this because of drop order on the unwind path? If `Foo` doesn't implement `Drop`, there's no conflict because we don't put `StorageDead`s in cleanup blocks. But if `Foo` does implement `Drop`, we end up with a drop for `foo` on the unwind path before the drop for the `(bar,)` temp due to Rust 2021 tail expr scopes. My idea was that we'd move out of that temp before it's a problem, but if we panic before then, that might not be the case.

I tested this hunch and it seems maybe correct? The conflicting location is the drop terminator for `foo` in a cleanup block. In contrast, for the reproducer in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/154988#issuecomment-4207324425 (i.e. for pre-https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/154994 `dbg!` and no `Drop` impl for `Foo`), the conflicting location was the `StorageDead` for `foo` on the happy path.

This really isn't something we should have to worry about in `dbg!`.. maybe it's time to give up on tricky solutions and just do it with `super let`? Though with `super let` in the state it's in right now it'd still be a bit tricky, unfortunately.
author: dianne

body: As for how we can end up unwinding between creating the `(bar,)` temporary and moving out of it, as far as I can tell it's because we first move `bar` into a temporary to be used as the operand for the tuple constructor, which is dropped immediately after constructing the tuple. Of course, this can't actually panic at runtime because it's always uninitialized at that point; aiui drop elaboration will replace that drop with a goto. But since borrowck happens first, the cfg still has that edge there (and I assume if we did move drop elaboration first, we'd use a `FalseUnwind` to keep the static semantics the same.. though I wouldn't say it's particularly easy to reason about this way).
author: dianne

body:
If I'm right about that, there's a more invasive way to fix this as well: we could make constructor operands not lead to hallucinated panics in borrowck by unscheduling their drops after the aggregate value is formed. Probably that's too subtle? It working the way it does feels like a weird emergent implementation artifact rather than intentional design, though.. it's pretty subtle either way.

I'll see if I can implement `dbg!` with `super let` in a way that doesn't fall prey to this. I'd still like to avoid `super let`, but I don't have other ideas at this point. Plus, in the future I think whatever replaces `super let` should be the go-to for these tricky macro scoping things; it should be more straightforward than wrangling `match` (hopefully!).

body: I believe it's the `drop(_7) -> [return: bb1, unwind: bb10];` at the end of `bb0`. If you get to `bb10`, you drop `_1` (`foo`) before `_6` (the `(Bar<'_>,)` temporary). However, `_7` (the operand to the tuple expression) has already been moved from in the statement immediately above that (when constructing the tuple value) so it's not *actually* going to panic. body:
There is a workaround available today, though it's a bit annoying: for every 1ZST token type `Tok` that you define and want other crates to be allowed to include in repr(transparent) wrappers, define:

```rust
#[repr(transparent)]
pub struct WithTok<T>(pub T, pub Tok);
```

Then downstream crates that want to put multiple such tokens in their own repr(transparent) wrappers can replace this:

```rust
#[repr(transparent)]
struct Wrapper<T>(T, lib1::Tok1, lib2::Tok2);
```

with this:

```rust
#[repr(transparent)]
struct Wrapper<T>(lib1::WithTok1<lib2::WithTok2<T>>);
```

This is a lot of boilerplate to construct and access, but it maintains the property that `Wrapper<T>` is a transparent wrapper around `T`, gives access to the token values in case they're non-trivial to construct, and reduces the API commitment problem to documenting that the various `WithTok<T>` types are transparent wrappers around `T` (which is less tricky when the fields are public).

This was changed in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/155473 cc @scottmcm

`#[repr(C)]` on a struct that contains non-`#[repr(C)]` is not sufficient to guarantee a fixed layout. You need to have `#[repr(C)]` or something similar on each of the field types recursively too. In particular, `Option` is not `#[repr(C)]`.

I'd say that your code is relying on something that's never been promised to be stable.

author: theemathas

Thanks for the answer

I'm surprised that there's no linting / warning for trying to put an Option in a `#[repr(C)]` struct then, because if I understand correctly there's no way anyone wants to do that.
author: aureliar8

body: `Option<NonNull<u8>>` (or with similarly defined-size pointees) and `Option<NonZeroU8>` both have stable representations, certainly in that they have a well-described `None` variant, and for various reasons are often used in `repr(C)` structs. So in order to lint without an enormous number of false positives, we would have to inspect every type and do a significant amount of reasoning about its *future possible variant encodings* for the sake of the lint. It *can* be done, but does anyone want to do it?
author: workingjubilee

body: Mind, we do have lints that do similar without reasoning to prevent false positives, and they are *wildly unpopular*.
author: workingjubilee

body:
Note that this is not just `Option` -- *any* repr(rust) in a `repr(C)` type has this.  `#[repr(C)] struct Foo(Vec<u32>);` doesn't give the `Vec` a guaranteed layout either, for example.

body:
Thanks @bjorn3 
 
As you pointed out, we can work around this issue through target registration, but there is a scalability limitation with that approach.
 
Even for the x86-64 architecture alone, we already maintain four different target combinations:
 
```
x86-64_oe-linux-gnu
x86-64_oesdk-linux-gnu
x86-64_oe-linux-musl
x86-64_oesdk-linux-musl
```
 
The same process would then need to be repeated across at least five additional architectures (arm, arm64, riscv64...)
 
In addition, Yocto is designed to support highly customized Linux distributions, where users commonly define their own target naming conventions. As a result, this approach would effectively require end users themselves to register and maintain their custom targets. For example:
 
```
x86-64_wrs-linux-gnu
aarch64_wrs-linux-gnu
```
 
These may further vary depending on their distribution.
 
As a result, the number of possible targets is effectively unbounded. Because of this, relying on target registration does not appear to be a scalable or practical solution for us.

We also explored using a wrapper function to automatically pass `-Zunstable-options` when invoking rustc as a workaround. However, this approach has several limitations within our project's sdk environment, making it unsuitable for adoption.

Given these constraints, would it be possible to limit the `-Zunstable-options` requirement specifically to cases where rustc is invoked to build for a custom target JSON file, rather than requiring it for all invocations?
For example:
```
./rustc --target custom-target.json -Zunstable-options # Here the -Zunstable-options required
./rustc -vV # Here the -Zunstable-options not required
```

@davidtwco  

Any suggestions on this approach?

@benozol can you explain at a higher level why you're expecting this or what you're hoping to achieve? This is expected behavior because Rust `*.a` staticlib files still depend on libc/standard APIs. For example if you compile for a native platform and produce a staticlib it's going to have undefined symbols for functions/data found in `libc.so` on your native system. (or something else on Windows).

The undefined `pthread_*` symbols are functions that the standard library is using from `libc.a`, provided in wasi-sdk as a standard wasi toolchain. Rust also ships with its own `libc.a`, but that's not included in a Rust staticlib since it's a "self contained sysroot" onl used during linking.

To guarantee this for time sources that have an unspecified epoch we'd need to store it on program startup for first use, which would add a bit of overhead. Otherwise the epoch could always be picked in the worst possible way, whether we use signed or unsigned time.

In posix the [epoch is unspecified](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/clock_getres.html). Linux promises that epoch = boottime (modulo suspends).

In the future we really want to allow splitting based on another `OsStr`, even if the other `OsStr` isn't valid UTF-8. This may lead to a slightly unexpected situation, e.g.:

```rust
os_str.strip_prefix(other_os_str); // works
os_str.split_at(other_os_str.len()); // might panic
```

A solution for splitting at platform-specific indexes would be to suggest using platform-specific functions (e.g. `as_bytes` and `from_bytes` on Unix, or adding a new `split_bytes_at` extension method).

Documentation could help here but I want to be clear what it would mean if these functions are stabilized since we would be committing to this in some regards.

author: joshtriplett

body:
A quick note for @rust-lang/libs-api as to _why_:

Integer, floating point, and pointer operations are implemented by the traits `SimdInt`, `SimdUint`, `SimdFloat`, `SimdConstPtr`, `SimdMutPtr`. This allows us to treat `Simd<T, N>` as a container. We can't implement element-specific directly on `Simd` without either negative trait bounds (e.g. `SimdInt: !SimdFloat`) or forgoing generics entirely.

Consider a function that takes element type `T` and returns element type `T::Type`. We have only 3 options:
* Use a trait associated type `type SimdOfType = Simd<T::Type, N>` and use the signature `fn foo(self) -> <Self as SimdTrait>::SimdOfType`. We don't really like this option.
    * Sometimes this causes type inference issues, and writing generics is much more difficult because you need bounds like `Vector: SimdOfTrait<SimdOfType = Simd<U, N>>`.
    * In real use, I have found these bounds to cover multiple associated types and often nest multiple projections to an impractical degree.
    * Documentation is difficult to read because the number of trait associated types explodes and the meaning is non-local.
* Use `min_generic_const_args`: `fn foo(self) -> Simd<T::Type, { Self::LENGTH }>`
    * This is a nice solution, though it does require the length to be a trait associated const.
    * It seems the MGCA feature is likely to remain experimental for a while and not suitable for use in core/std
* Use receiver `self: Simd<Self, N>`: Separates the type and length generics, allowing `fn foo<const N: usize>(self: Simd<Self, N>) -> Simd<Self::Type, N>`.
    * Each function must be generic over length rather than just each impl block.
    * No technical reason we cannot use today.
    * Clear function signatures.
    * Implementing traits over the element type rather than vector type slightly simplifies some existing parts of the API that care about specific element types.
author: calebzulawski

body:
Have you considered providing a trait alias (AKA, a trait variant)?  This would clean up the bounds by letting use sites assume the shape of these associated types.  With this, we can write, e.g.:

```rust
fn round_trip<T: FloatElement, const N: usize>(x: Simd<T, N>) -> Simd<T, N>
where
    Simd<T, N>: SimdFloatVec<T, N>,
{
    let bits = x.to_bits();
    let signed = bits.cast_signed();
    signed.cast_float()
}
```

<details>
<summary>(What it looks like without this.)</summary>

```rust
fn round_trip<T: SimdElement, const N: usize>(x: Simd<T, N>) -> Simd<T, N>
where
  Simd<T, N>: SimdFloat,
  <Simd<T, N> as SimdFloat>::Bits:
    SimdUint<Signed = <Simd<T, N> as SimdFloat>::SignedInt>,
  <Simd<T, N> as SimdFloat>::SignedInt:
    SimdInt<Float = Simd<T, N>>,
{
  let bits = x.to_bits();
  let signed = bits.cast_signed();
  signed.cast_float()
}
```
</details>

<details>
<summary>Another option.</summary>

If we really want rid of that `Simd<T, N>: SimdFloatVec<T, N>` bound, could we do it [like this][ex-2] without using `Receiver`?
</details>

(If we ever went further with implied bounds, e.g., https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2089, then the `T: FloatElement` bound would no longer be needed.)

Here's a fully-worked example: [Playground link][ex-1].

How much would this help?  Are there any language / type system features you'd want to make that better?

Similarly, have you considered putting the generic parameters directly on the vector traits (e.g., `SimdFloat`)?  What are the tradeoffs of that?

[ex-1]: https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&code=%2F%2F+This+demonstrates+applying+the+trait+alias+pattern+to+traits+for%0A%2F%2F+the+%60Simd%3CT%2C+N%3E%60+type.++The+idea+is+that+for+each+vector+trait%2C%0A%2F%2F+we+have+the+base+variant+%28e.g.%2C+%60SimdFloat%60%29+that+is+meant+to+be%0A%2F%2F+implemented+%28and+has+no+generic+parameters%29+and+a+use-site+variant%0A%2F%2F+%28e.g.%2C+%60SimdFloatVec%3CT%2C+N%3E%60%29.%0A%2F%2F%0A%2F%2F+The+problem+this+solves+is+that%2C+otherwise%2C+a+projection%0A%2F%2F+such+as+%60%3CSimd%3CT%2C+N%3E+as+SimdFloat%3E%3A%3AMask%60+does+not+carry+any%0A%2F%2F+shape+information.++I.e.%2C+the+use+site+can%27t+assume+that+the%0A%2F%2F+mask+is+%60Mask%3CT%3A%3AMask%2C+N%3E%60+unless+it+adds+this+predicate%2C%0A%2F%2F+creating+unwieldy+bounds.%0A%2F%2F%0A%2F%2F+Having+the+use+site+instead+use+the+trait+alias+solves+this%2C+as+the%0A%2F%2F+trait+alias+constrains+the+shape+of+these+associated+types.%0A%2F%2F%0A%2F%2F+See%3A%0A%2F%2F%0A%2F%2F+-+https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Frust-lang%2Frust%2Fissues%2F156270%0A%2F%2F%0A%2F%2F+Author%3A+TC%0A%2F%2F+Date%3A+2026-05-20%0A%0A%23%21%5Ballow%28dead_code%29%5D%0A%0Apub+trait+SimdElement%3A+Sized+%2B+Copy+%7B%0A++++type+Mask%3A+SimdElement%3B%0A%7D%0A%0Aimpl+SimdElement+for+f32+%7B%0A++++type+Mask+%3D+i32%3B%0A%7D%0Aimpl+SimdElement+for+i32+%7B%0A++++type+Mask+%3D+i32%3B%0A%7D%0Aimpl+SimdElement+for+u32+%7B%0A++++type+Mask+%3D+i32%3B%0A%7D%0A%0Apub+trait+FloatElement%3A+SimdElement+%7B%0A++++type+Bits%3A+SimdElement%3CMask+%3D+Self%3A%3AMask%3E%0A++++++++%2B+UintElement%3CSigned+%3D+Self%3A%3ASignedInt%3E%3B%0A++++type+SignedInt%3A+SimdElement%3CMask+%3D+Self%3A%3AMask%3E%0A++++++++%2B+IntElement%3CFloat+%3D+Self%3E%3B%0A%7D%0Aimpl+FloatElement+for+f32+%7B%0A++++type+Bits+%3D+u32%3B%0A++++type+SignedInt+%3D+i32%3B%0A%7D%0A%0Apub+trait+IntElement%3A+SimdElement+%7B%0A++++type+Float%3A+SimdElement%3CMask+%3D+Self%3A%3AMask%3E%3B%0A++++type+Unsigned%3A+SimdElement%3CMask+%3D+Self% body:
I looked more closely at `compiler/rustc_monomorphize/src/collector.rs`, and I think the issue is not that the recursion-limit check is missing, but that it only measures recursive instantiation depth.

It appears that `check_recursion_limit` tracks instantiation depth keyed by `DefId`, incrementing it by exactly 1 at each recursive call. Since the default `recursion_limit` is 128, the collector considers early depths to be perfectly safe.

However, for non-regular recursion like A -> (A, A), the type size grows exponentially. By depth ~25, the type tree already contains millions of nodes. The compiler likely hangs while folding, hashing, or interning this massive type tree _long before_ it reaches the 128 depth limit.

---

**A potential idea for a fix:**
Perhaps the collector could eagerly enforce the `type_length_limit` on `instance.args` during the recursion check, rather than relying solely on the linear depth limit. Checking the type's structural size before proceeding with expensive MIR substitutions might successfully catch this exponential blowup and emit a proper limit diagnostic.

Thanks for your time looking into this!

body:
> The issue is in `std::sys::thread::current()` (specifically `init_current()`) — it unconditionally sets `CURRENT` on the _calling_ thread's TLS, regardless of whether that thread is owned by the Rust runtime. When `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH` fires on a _foreign_ thread (e.g., Vulkan Loader's internal thread), Rust's std pollutes `CURRENT` on that thread's TLS. Later, when `std::thread::spawn` creates a new thread, `set_current()` in the _new_ thread (not the foreign thread) detects `CURRENT` is already `Some` and aborts.

That's not quite correct. `CURRENT` is thread-local, so there can be no cross-thread pollution. The issue is that the thread initialisation logic run on new threads spawned by `thread::spawn` assumes that it is the first thing run on the thread, and thus `CURRENT` cannot be initialised. As you correctly point out, a lot of things in `std` can initialise `CURRENT`, calling any of them in response to `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH` will lead to the crash you encountered. 

To me, this falls under the category of [using `std` before main](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html#use-before-and-after-main); we provide support for that on a best-effort basis. In this case however, fixing the issue seems exceedingly difficult – we need `CURRENT` to be set to the handle created by `spawn` (otherwise thread names wouldn't get set), but it's not a good idea to change an existing handle, as thread handles (and especially thread IDs) aren't supposed to change during the lifetime of a thread.

Let's keep this open, perhaps there's a solution I haven't thought of...

body:
One should note this advisory by Microsoft about code going into DllMain:

> There are significant limits on what you can safely do in a DLL entry point. See [General Best Practices](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dlls/dynamic-link-library-best-practices) for specific Windows APIs that are unsafe to call in DllMain. If you need anything but the simplest initialization then do that in an initialization function for the DLL. You can require applications to call the initialization function after DllMain has run and before they call any other functions in the DLL.

This may not seem like much of a caveat, but then if one consults the General Best Practices in question, one finds this sentence:

> The ideal [DllMain](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dlls/dllmain) would be just an empty stub.

...And while it does then immediately acknowledge that just an empty stub is not always viable, it does continue on with explaining details of how you should defer most real work.

It only blesses the following tasks:
> Initialize static data structures and members at compile time.
> Create and initialize synchronization objects.
> Allocate memory and initialize dynamic data structures (avoiding the functions listed above.)
> Set up thread local storage (TLS).
> Open, read from, and write to files.
> Call functions in Kernel32.dll (except the functions that are listed above).
> Set global pointers to NULL, putting off the initialization of dynamic members. In Microsoft Windows Vista™, you can use the one-time initialization functions to ensure that a block of code is executed only once in a multithreaded environment.

As one might guess by it referring to Vista like it is a new entity, the "best practices" here is from 2006, so it is very likely quite dated. However, I have often observed new limitations on OS APIs being a primary feature of more recent OS updates, rather than the opposite.

Creating a thread, by the way, is explicitly prohibited. So creating a worker thread inside DllMain if the message is `DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH`, like you plan on doing, is not OS-supported behavior. If it works, of course, I'm not exactly going to stop you, but it does raise the question of what exactly we should be fixing if the OS isn't interested in blessing this pattern either.

body:
I think what's going on is that coherence uses the new solver and the new solver also just doesn't support GCE and currently things are being changed about how normalization works in the new solver (which affects coherence). In theory GCE should only be more broken when it comes to const arguments in impl headers, but I do agree that it's significantly more broken now than it was before which is quite unfortunate ^^'

I think `generic_const_args` is "ready" enough for people to migrate off of GCE to it at this point and generally is what people should do as GCE won't stick around for much longer, regardless of the fact that its support has been gradually degrading over the last couple years. Given this, I don't think GCE is important enough to revert or block any of the work happening around normalization in the new solver, but yeah sorry for GCE kinda falling apart.

Would you be able to open a thread in [#project-const-generics](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/260443-project-const-generics) on the rust zulip titled sth like "help migrating from GCE to GCA"? I (and others) will be able to help you with migrating from GCE to GCA. 

Other than that, the diagnositc you're getting sure is unfortunate 😅 does not set you up for success (i will file a bug for this). The way GCA works is that it allows arbitrary paths to const items including generics. so you can do `const FOO<T>: usize = size_of::<T>();` and then `[u8; FOO<T>]` but you can't do `[u8; size_of::<T>()]`.

body: This is working as intended. The type `i32` implements the `Copy` trait. This changes how moving values with this type behaves. Instead of making the old place unusable, the old place is now usable, and you end up with two copies of the same value. See https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Copy.html

Assoc const bindings are likely also affected.

I mean intuitively it makes sense, in rustdoc we don't run all analysis passes for function bodies and suddenly we're querying `typeck` while the surrounding code isn't properly "set up" like here containing anon consts not having been query-fed which would usually happen during HIR ty lowering / HIR typeck.

More specifically `typeck` on anon consts immediately calls `type_of` which wasn't fed yet. I don't know where/when it should've been fed: During type collection (`rustc_hir_analysis::collect`)? At some point during HIR typeck? No idea.

body:
I have a feeling that we can't request the lowering of anon consts *on demand* / *selectively*, i.e., without unconditionally running some extra rustc analysis pass top-down which would trash performance by orders of magnitude.

So I'm thinking of just "poisoning" anon consts when visiting nested bodies using the `SpanMapVisitor` to prevent us from calling `typeck` when encountering type-dependent definitions until we have found a better solution.

author: cathaysia

body:
> however, I noticed that no bounds checking is being performed at this specific location. That is why I created this issue. Or perhaps this behavior was intentionally designed this way?

In fact, there is a boundary check here that is implicitly generated by the compiler to prevent further undefined behaviors, and that is why you can see this panic message.

According to [the doc of `getrandom`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrandom.2.html), it should not return a value greater than the buffer length. Therefore, not performing explicit boundary checks here and converting to recoverable errors also sounds reasonable.

I would suggest narrowing the problem down by creating a reproducible code snippet, and then we can further investigate the cause together.

body:
> the execution environment is MIPS64o32

o32 is for MIPS32, MIPS64's 32-bit ABI is called n32.

The syscall numbers for MIPS64 differ between 32-bit and 64-bit, and Rust supports only 64-bit targets. Unless you are using a properly patched version of std/libc, you are likely calling system calls with the wrong syscall numbers.

tl;dr Any basic color choice may be fine, maybe green as if a "green light."

Accessibility/color blindness assumption: (Based on a quick online/AI query, simplified, no knowledge of the subject; please correct this if needed): It seems that there is no _single_ "basic/mainstream" color that, when used as "pure/intense" for text foreground, would be invisible/difficult for the same person on *both* white background and black background (with no other colors nearby).

Also
- major terminals/window managers/IDE's offer choice of background colors/themes, so there should be a way to workaround, as far as we don't use various non-black and non-white colors next to each other/contrasting with each other.
- in Mac OS/Linux/Unix terminals/shells (and maybe in Windows Powershell, too), one can pipe the outputs (including error output) to a file, or to another command (like `cat`), which removes any color/formatting control escapes.
- `cargo build` (and friends) take `--color never` parameter, like `cargo build --color never`; or, you can set the environment variable `CARGO_TERM_COLOR=never`. That does _not_ work completely; for now you need to use `cargo test --color=never -- --color=never` (and friends), give thumbs up to [rust-lang/cargo#1983](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/1983).

The above generalization is not to discard/minimize needs of people with visual difficulties, but to be realistic about what we can provide, and what workarounds exist already.

See also
- "We use basic ANSI styles": [rust-lang/cargo#2290#issuecomment-1728318644](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/2290#issuecomment-1728318644),
- "prefer we stick to the basic colors " [rust-lang/cargo#2290#issuecomment-1885757580](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/2290#issuecomment-1885757580)
author: peter-lyons-kehl

body:
> * in Mac OS/Linux/Unix terminals/shells (and maybe in Windows Powershell, too), one can pipe the outputs (including error output) to a file, or to another command (like `cat`), which removes any color/formatting control escapes.

Not sure if you meant it how it sounds, but the colours are controlled by the original tool that generates the text, not removed by the terminal, file, or command the output is piped to.

Tools can auto-detect whether they are writing to a terminal and disable coloured output. This requires the cooperation of the colour/terminal library, terminal app, and/or the OS. That's what happens when redirecting output, the command or file is detected as "not a terminal", so the tool doesn't output colour escapes.

Sometimes the detection doesn't work, and users will see raw output with colour codes in it (in tools that escape control codes). This can be rendered as colours using `less --raw-control-chars` or similar.

Below is an analysis from Claude. I don't vouche for its accuracy, but it seems plausible based on the disassembly I did myself. Core dump analysis Crash summary Signal: SIGSEGV at 0x0000564f732edcd0 Self pointer (`Option>`): 0x7f9ea51f9130 Memory there: 0x7f9ea51f9130: 0xffffffffffffffff 0x00000000000000b4 0x7f9ea51f9140: 0x00007f9e84000030 0x00000000000000a0 The first word is 0xffffffffffffffff — the None niche value. The disassembled crash sequence (inlined as_ref) as_ref was inlined into the collect closure. The relevant instructions: ``` ; Load the first 8 bytes of Option> (the niche/discriminant word) 0x...dcce: mov 0x150(%rsp),%rax ; rax = 0xffffffffffffffff (None niche) ; Truncate to 32-bit → ecx = 0xffffffff 0x...dcce: mov %eax,%ecx ; ecx = 0xffffffff ; *** CRASH HERE *** ; Speculative table load using ecx as an unvalidated scaled index ; Effective address = rsp + 0x160 + (0xffffffff × 8) = way out of range 0x...dcd0: mov 0x160(%rsp,%rcx,8),%r8 ; ← SIGSEGV ; This check comes TOO LATE — it would have branched to None 0x...dcd8: cmp $0xffffffffffffffff,%rax 0x...dcdc: je ``` ---- Type layout and the niche optimization ``` Cow layout (32 bytes): offset 0: u64 — discriminant: 0 = Borrowed, 1 = Owned offset 8: ptr — (Borrowed: &str data ptr) | (Owned: String buf ptr) offset 16: u64 — (Borrowed: &str len) | (Owned: String len) offset 24: u64 — (Borrowed: padding/undef) | (Owned: String cap) ``` Niche optimization for `Option>`: Cow's discriminant only uses values 0 and 1. All other bit patterns are niches — impossible values. The compiler picks 0xffffffffffffffff (= u64::MAX) as the None niche, stored in the discriminant word. This avoids the cost of a separate Option tag — the `Option>` has the same size as `Cow` itself (32 bytes). ---- Exactly which instruction caused the SIGSEGV ``` 0x0000564f732edcd0: mov 0x160(%rsp,%rcx,8),%r8 ``` The compiler is doing a speculative load from a local stack table before checking whether the Option is None. It uses ecx (the lower 32 bits of the niche discriminant) as a scaled index. With the None niche value loaded, ecx = 0xffffffff, so the effective address becomes: ``` rsp + 0x160 + (0xffffffff × 8) = 0x7f9ea51f8fe0 + 0x160 + 0x7fffffff8 ≈ 0x7f9e251f9138 ← unmapped → SIGSEGV ``` The cmp/je check that would have branched safely to the None path appears after the fault — too late. This is a compiler bug: a speculative load is emitted using an unvalidated index that can be the niche sentinel value, which produces an out-of-range address and faults before the None guard is ever reached. ---- Old binary (LLVM 21) — buggy sequence ``` ; Load Option> discriminant word +10494: mov 0x150(%rsp),%rax ; rax = 0xffffffffffffffff (None niche) +10494: mov %eax,%ecx ; ecx = 0xffffffff (truncated!) ; *** CRASH: speculative table load BEFORE None check *** +10496: mov 0x160(%rsp,%rcx,8),%r8 ; addr = rsp+0x160 + 0xffffffff*8 → SIGSEGV ; None check comes too late +10508: cmp $0xffffffffffffffff,%rax +10508: je ``` ---- New binary (LLVM 22) — fixed sequence ``` ; Load Option> discriminant word (via pointer this time) +452: mov 0x2a0(%rsi),%rax ; rax = discriminant ; *** None check comes FIRST — before any use of rax as index *** +459: cmp $0xffffffffffffffff,%rax +463: je ; safe branch, no memory touched ; Only reaches here if Some — now safely inspect the Cow variant +469: test %rax,%rax ; discriminant == 0 → Borrowed? +472: je ; simple branch, no scaled-index load ``` ---- What changed | | Old | New | |---|---|---| | None check order | After speculative load | Before any use of discriminant | | Dispatch method | Scaled-index table load (mov (%rsp,%rcx,8)) | Simple test/je branches | | Crash possible? | Yes — niche 0xffffffff as u32 index ×8 overflows | No — None exits before any index arithmetic | The fix ensures the cmp $0xffffffffffffffff guard is evaluated before the discriminant value is used as a scaled index. The new code also replaces the indexed-table dispatch with plain conditional branches (test %rax,%rax; je), which are safe regardless of what value rax holds.

> Note: Allocators are allowed to panic in Rust:
>
> >   Implementations are encouraged to return Err on memory exhaustion rather than panicking or aborting, but this is not a strict requirement. (Specifically: it is legal to implement this trait atop an underlying native allocation library that aborts on memory exhaustion.)

This seems like an incorrect conclusion, the part that you've quoted specifically says *abort*, not unwinding panic.  It is currently an open question as to whether the allocator itself is permitted to panic (among other potential problematic behavior, see https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines/issues/506)

Edit: actually I suppose it does mention panicking as a potential error strategy, but this seems contradictory to existing open questions.

body:
As a general principle, the compiler intentionally never uses the condition of an `if`, or any other *value* of an expression or variable, as part of deciding whether to accept or reject a program. So, it does not matter that `first_encounter` is only `false` when `following_token` is initialized.

However, the diagnostic could be improved: since it is already talking about things like “if the `if` condition is `false`”, it could reasonably include a “note:” specifying that the compiler is not actually analyzing whether that condition could ever be relevantly false, just describing a hypothetical situation.

body:
As part of the attribute parsing rework we moved many checks that were done at various points during compilation to check_attr, but this pass works on hir, so after macro expansion.

Presumably any attribute that checks their target at https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/main/compiler/rustc_passes/src/check_attr.rs#L172 does not handle macro invocations correctly (this includes repr).

Similarly,
```rust
#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented(message = "baz")]
produce_trait!(X);
```
has always silently done nothing. But I changed diagnostic attributes to do their target checking during attribute parsing and (unknowingly) fixed it to emit a warning.

>

> 
> I suspect this is a RISC-V hardware implementation bug, considering that there have been known reports of defects about floating-point in certain RISC-V hardware, and also RISC-V ISA previously modified the definitions of `fmin` and `fmax` instructions in [riscv/riscv-isa-manual#75](https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual/pull/75) -- before ISA v2.2 they implement IEEE 754-2008 `minNum` and `maxNum`, since ISA v2.2 they implement IEEE 754-2019 `minimumNumber` and `maximumNumber`.


Thanks for the excellent explanations. I confirm this bug is a false positive. I did not reproduce this on another riscv64 [hardware](https://www.sifive.cn/boards/hifive-premier-p550).

body:
This is likely a direct consequence of us doing promotion on MIR -- we don't actually know which expression was in which scope, we just check whether the things that are actually used to compute the `&<expr>` can all be promoted. We've been idly saying for a while that promotion should really be a HIR or THIR transform that introduces `const` blocks but that's a big change likely involving lots of breakage -- so far nobody seemed able and motivated to do this. I'd be happy to support this from the MIR / const-eval side but don't know enough about HIR or THIR to be the main driver / mentor.

body:
Okay, I think I found what is happening (though not why).

Looking at the debug output of rustc, the `depth` of the obligations is steadily increasing (upwards of 30000).

In `process_obligation`, if the obligations predicate has aliases, a new obligation with the normalized predicate is pushed, with an increased depth value. And `ProcessResult::Changed` is returned [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/35143615544ede08a47947901cd4a6b7c5ecd450/compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/traits/fulfill.rs#L413).

All of this happens before any recursion depth check is ever performed.

But if a predicate can be infinitely normalized (for whatever reason I do not understand), the recursion limit is never checked before returning. So if I understand this correctly, it could run infinitely.

I think the recursion limit is only checked [later](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/35143615544ede08a47947901cd4a6b7c5ecd450/compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/traits/fulfill.rs#L604)

author: jorendorff

body:
Looking at this again, adding the semicolon at the back of the `}` would not fix the issue because the problem is the fact that an `if` expression without an `else` should always produce `()`. In this case, `page.method()` returns a `usize`.

Normally, adding the semicolon was supposed to discard the value of the `if` expression, thereby making this work. However, the compiler will first type-check the `if` expression before considering the outer semicolon.

The Rust compiler sees a mismatch because an `if` expression without an `else` is expected to evaluate to `()`, but the branch is producing a `usize`. Therefore, the compiler emits an error before it gets to the point where the outer semicolon could discard the value.

This suggestion is more of a support suggestion that would not work without the first suggestion. It is explicing telling the compiler to discard the value produce by the if expression. Rewording of the help sentence could be better, not having it also works. 

```
help: consider using a semicolon here
  |
8 |     };
  |      +
```

it is not helpful here. 

cc: @mejrs  and @estebank 

The issue heading should be change though from -> Syntactically incorrect code suggestion for missing semicolon in if without else to something like `Unhelpful/confusing additional code suggestion for missing semicolon`

body:
I guess the question is, is the address of a pointer outside its provenance defined? It compiles correctly with `(x as *const i32).addr() - 4` instead of `(x as *const i32).wrapping_sub(1).addr()`.

The Rust docs does guarantee that `wrapping_sub` can temporarily go out of the provenance and go back in, but I'm not sure if any guarantees are made about the address you would get from an out-of-provenance pointer.
author: orlp

body:
Yes the address of a pointer is always well-defined and entirely unaffected by its provenance. This is an instance of the known LLVM problems around provenance.

Maybe we should compile `addr()` to `ptrtoint` to partially mitigate this for now? @nikic
author: RalfJung

body:
@RalfJung We already do that. We don't actually use ptrtoaddr for addr().

The issue in this sample is the usual int2ptr(ptr2int(x)) one. (Which, I think, is the first one we should address after byte type implementation is complete.)

body:
I've been digging into this. The ICE comes from `compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/regions.rs` when building the `OutlivesEnvironment` during wf checking.

Here's the cycle:
1. `new_with_implied_bounds_compat` iterates param_env bounds and deeply normalizes each `TypeOutlives` predicate
2. For `Foo: 'static`, the solver enters `normalize_free_alias`, which adds `predicates_of(Foo)` as sub-goals, and that includes `Foo: 'static` itself
3. Proving `Foo: 'static` requires normalizing `Foo` again, which creates a cycle and normalization fails
4. `delayed_bug` fires, but `trivial_bounds` suppressed the overflow error that would otherwise exist, so there's no real error to back it up. ICE.

The fix I'm working on replaces the `delayed_bug` with `continue` (skip the bound on normalization failure). If normalization fails due to a real error, that error was already emitted during obligation evaluation in `enter_wf_checking_ctxt`. If it fails due to a self-referential cycle like this, the bound doesn't contribute useful region information anyway.

One thing I keep thinking about though: should the next solver be able to handle this cycle without failing in the first place? Right now the where-clause goals in `normalize_free_alias` use `GoalSource::Misc`, which maps to `PathKind::Unknown`, which means ambiguity on cycle. It feels like there's a longer-term question about how `TypeOutlives` goals interact with alias normalization. Ideally, proving `Foo: 'static` shouldn't need to re-normalize `Foo` when we're already in the middle of normalizing it.

Curious what you think about this approach. Would also like to hear if anyone on the types team has thoughts on the solver-level interaction here.
