body:
> The difference in the MIR is where the control flow goes if the destructor of `Bar` panics (`drop(_7)` in `bb0`). This destructor seems to be, for some reason, ran immediately after `Bar` is moved into the tuple.

That drop is for the temporary that holds the tuple constructor's operand: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/destructors.html#operands. It's not actually run, since that temporary is moved out of immediately (drop elaboration should turn it into a goto), but borrowck doesn't seem to ignore dead unwind edges so it's effectively treated as if it can panic.

In `fails`, unwinding from `drop(_7)` drops the temporary holding the match scrutinee before `foo`, due to pre-2024 tail expression scoping.

In `works`, we seemingly skip dropping the scrutinee when unwinding from `drop(_7)`? There's two separate unwind paths there, whereas normally they're joined together in a tree (like in `fails`): unwinding from `drop(_7)` drops `_2`, then `_1` (i.e. `bar`, then `foo`, leaving the scrutinee un-dropped), but unwinding elsewhere drops `_2`, then `_1`, *then `_6`*" (i.e. `bar`, then `foo`, *then the scrutinee*, as expected). When leaving the scope for the tuple expression, (i.e. when the drop for `_7` is built), `_6`'s `DropKind::Value` drop isn't scheduled, so it doesn't end up in the drop tree. Temporaries' `DropKind::Value` drops are only scheduled after lowering the expression being put into the temporary. Usually (and in `fails`) this is fine: when we leave the tuple expression, we've scheduled the drop for `_6`, so if `_7`'s drop panics, `_6` is dropped. In `works`, we leave the tuple expression (i.e. we build the drop for `_7`) before leaving the expression being put into the temporary (i.e. the block), so `_6`'s drop hasn't yet been scheduled when building the unwind drops for `_7`'s drop.

I'll have to think about whether this can cause drops to be forgotten on unwind paths that can actually be run.

It seems the warning slips through because the `deployment_mismatch` filter only matches the older ld format for object files:

`ld: warning: object file (...) was built for newer 'macOS' version (...) than being linked (...)`

The format in this issue (`ld: building for macOS-11.0, but linking with dylib '...' which was built for newer version 15.0`) is from newer Apple ld and isn't caught by that filter — or anywhere else in the codebase. So instead of being downgraded to `linker_info` (Allow by default), it goes through as a full `linker_messages` warning.

I think I can put up a PR to extend the filter to also cover this dylib variant to fix this issue?

I don't think it makes a lot of sense to me as an end user. I have a generic constant, I have what is, essentially, a function that converts `u32` to `usize` with some logic. It either returns `usize` or it panics at compile time (or it enters infinite loop and is aborted at some point).

Whether any of that happens depends on the call site, it doesn't need to be known beforehand, it is totally fine that not all `u32` values are valid and is in fact possible that the constant will panic for certain invalid values.

For me it appears to be as constrained as plain `const SIZE: usize` would have been.

The fact that even this doesn't compile with the same error:
```rust
type const USIZE_TO_USIZE<const N: usize>: usize = const { N };

trait Trait {}

impl<const SIZE: usize, T> Trait for [T; USIZE_TO_USIZE::<SIZE>] {}
```

Is really disappointing.

In certain cases it is often desirable to use smaller than `usize` types, but not being able to cast back to `usize` results in awkward APIs that are not as misuse-resistant as they could have been.
author: nazar-pc

body:
Besides the potential for overlapping impls, rustc also *has to* be able to, for a given type, answer the question “does this type implement this trait”, without reference to exactly how the type was spelled in the source code — anything else would be unsound. That is, there has to be a deterministic algorithm for answering the question “does `[T; N]` implement `Trait`?”.

So, if `impl<const SIZE: u32, T> Trait for [T; U32_TO_USIZE::<SIZE>]` were to be valid, rustc would have to be able to *invert the function `U32_TO_USIZE`* — for each `N: usize` encountered, find a `SIZE: u32` value such that `U32_TO_USIZE::<SIZE> == N` (if one exists). It’s unlikely that Rust will ever include the functionality of inverting user-defined functions as part of type-and-trait-checking.

body:
I've got some further clues.

- macOS's `libunwind` is failing to unwind the stack, because it cannot find unwind info for the function `__rustc::rust_panic`.
- On macOS, there are two formats for unwinding:
  - Standard DWARF call-frame information, which goes in the `__eh_frame` section
  - Apple's [Compact Unwinding](https://faultlore.com/blah/compact-unwinding/) format, which is simpler and smaller but only valid for a subset of functions. This goes in the `__unwind_info` section.
- `__rustc::rust_panic` uses compact unwinding. **On the bad binary, the `__unwind_info` section is missing.**
- It appears rustc emits compact unwinding tables in the `__compact_unwind` section of intermediate .o files, which are then merged by the linker to produce the `__unwind_info` section.
- So, I suspect that whatever the "GCC linker" is does not know it needs to do this.

regarding that last bullet point: I don't know what the "GCC linker" is. There aren't that many linkers targeting macOS; there's Apple's ld64, LLVM's lld, some new closed-source Apple thing apparently, and maybe one or two other experimental/new linkers? Surely any moderately recent linker from Apple or LLVM will know how to correctly produce the `__unwind_info` section. So my best guess is that either your GCC distribution is shipping some ancient obsolete linker, or it's configuring it weirdly.

body:
Turns out that merely having a very long string literal is sufficient to cause unsoundness. No macros are needed.

To demonstrate this, I generated a rust program with the following script:
```python
with open("src/lib.rs", "w") as f:
    f.write('pub fn foo() -> usize { "')
    f.write(" " * 4_000_000_000)
    f.write('".len() }')
```

That is, the rust program looks like:
```rust
pub fn foo() -> usize { "(4 billion spaces here)".len() }
```

Compiling the program with `cargo build --target=i686-unknown-linux-gnu` produced no errors.

body:
We use rename for output files to atomically replace them. Having a copying fallback can cause concurrent rustc instances to crash while reading partially written crate metadata. And incremental compilation needs to finalize the entire incremental session in a single atomic operation by renaming a directory. Copying will both hurt performance and enable corruption that will cause people to report bugs that are indistinguishable from actual bugs in the incr comp support and thus cause extra work triaging them.

To me it seems like the reason `LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_REFER` exists at all rather than being unconditionally enabled is because when the v1 landlock abi was introduced, it wasn't known yet how to implement rename in a way that wouldn't enable sandbox escapes.

body:
There are a few different favors of Sample PGO (or AutoFDO) in Clang. In the original version (debug info based), Profi is not enabled by default. However, Profi is enabled by default for CSSPGO (context-sestive) or Probe-based SamplePGO.

The version we used in kernel build is FS-AFDO -- this is based on the original Sample PGO (debuginfo based).

In our AutoFDO patch to upstream kernel, we did not enable Profi.  We observed this degradation in userland
applications. As you probably know, FS-AFDO is widely deployed at Google for user applications.  Adding Profi on top did not yield improvements; instead, it resulted in a slight performance regression.

We have a theory about this, but we haven't yet had the opportunity to verify or address it.

That said, we haven't tested this in the kernel since measuring performance there is significantly more difficult than in user
applications. If there is evidence that Profi enhances kernel performance, we would be happy to include this option.

-Rong

body:
> Ah. My information was outdated and I wasn't aware of that PR. So you
are right, profi is on by default for clang, and I see the rationale
for enabling it for rust as well.

Thanks for checking and proving, that my understanding is right :)

> That said, I'm unclear on the decision to implement this within clang
specifically. My approach would have been to handle it in LLVM by
setting the internal option to true by default, which would avoid the
need for changes across every front end.

Fair point. If LLVM believes that this change is good for improving debuginfo-based Sample PGO in general (in general, not in all cases as you mentioned) - I think it would be nice to see it enabled there. I guess one of the reasons for the way it was implemented is that people actually doesn't care much about Sample PGO besides Clang nowadays. Sample PGO is relatively "hidden" technique at all, and with other compilers besides Clang it's almost in a non-existent state.

Knowing all the context above, I see multiple ways how we can proceed further with this issue.

### 1. Do not enable Profi by default for Sample PGO in Rustc

We simply leave the things as they are currently implemented in Rustc.

Pros:

* We don't need to change anything in the Rustc source code. However, enabling Profi by default should be kinda trivial task to do since it requires only passing an additional LLVM flag during the LLVM invocation inside Rustc
* For use cases, where Profi makes things worse (as @xur-llvm mentioned above) we don't need to implement a way to **disable** Profi. E.g. if we enable Profi by default, Rust-in-Linux will be required to pass some additional flag to disable Profi (see the kernel [patch](https://lore.kernel.org/rust-for-linux/20260331-autofdo-v2-1-eb5c5964820d@google.com/)) - and such a flag doesn't exist yet either in Rustc - we will need to implement it.
* We leave room for improvements for the future. E.g. what if we decide to enable FS-AFDO approach by default instead of Profi in Rustc (see the 3rd option below)? Or provide two options at the same time to choose from. There are a variety of options here.

Cons:

* Our behaviour stays a bit different from Clang for the default Sample PGO case since **by default** Sample PGO in Clang will work a bit differently from Rustc. E.g. it influences Clang PGO guide reusability with Rustc (in ideal world, it shouldn't be even the case, but it is what it is for now)
* For use cases, where Profi improves Sample PGO efficiency (see my initial message in the topic), users will not get Profi-provided improvements **by default**. They will need to learn somehow about Profi existence (it means we'll need to update Rustc's PGO guide), pass flags properly, etc. - it makes Sample PGO developer experience a bit worse by default.

 ### 2. Enable Profi by default for Sample PGO in Rustc

With this approach, we enable Profi by default for Sample PGO in Rustc and make it consistent with Clang's behaviour.

Pros:

* Sample PGO users in Rustc will get benefits from Profi by default. It improves developers experience by default since they don't need to learn yet another hack to make Sample PGO a bit better.
* We stay in sync with Clang behaviour. It's a nice thing since Clang nowadays actually can/should be treated as a "reference LLVM frontend regarding PGO things" since most PGO developments are mostly done for C++ with Clang (thanks Google for the contribution).

Cons:

* It requires some implementation efforts. However, I don't expect anything significant here.
* For use cases, where Profi makes things worse, we will need to implement a way to disable it (see the Google case above). It could be a Rustc flag.

### 3. Enable FS-AFDO approach by default for Sample PGO in Rustc instead of Profi

This is a new option, where we instead of copying Clang behaviour choose another direction and enable FS-AFDO approach (with LLVM discriminators) by default instead of Profi. I would like to hear @xur-llvm about this one since I personally don't have much experience with this approach at the moment.

Pros:

* That's the way how Sample PGO is used inside Google - the largest Sample PGO user in the world nowadays, so we can trust pretty much their experience and feedback about this decision. Even if it's done mostly with Clang and C++ - the experience is totally applicable for the Rust case as well.
* Sample PGO users in Rustc will get benefits from FS-AFDO by default without needing to learn about yet another bunch of LLVM flags, ways how to pass it, etc. - it improves developers experience with Sample PGO by default.

Cons:

* Rustc becomes even more different from Clang regarding chosen defaults. It could lead to some surprises in the future regarding reusing Clang's Sample PGO experience/benches/etc. for Rustc.
* This option is not implemented anywhere **by default** so it's a bit more risky. I don't even know right now, is it a viable option or not. E.g. why it wasn't implemented by default in Clang instead of Profi? I don't have information about it - mayeb @xur-llvm can help here as well :)
* We need to implement it in Rustc somehow. As far as I understand, it shouldn't be a difficult task but anyway.

-------------------

Knowing all the context above, I suggest start with the first option - "1. Do not enable Profi by default for Sample PGO in Rustc". It gives all Rust users flexibility regarding ways of doing Sample PGO: someone will choose Sample PGO + Profi, someone will choose Sample PGO via FS-AFDO way, someone can even stay with a regular Sample PGO. TL;DR we leave the Sample PGO features additive as we can.

One important thing is that we definitely need to document all of these details/nuances with different Sample PGO flavours in the Rustc Sample PGO documentation. If we agree with this approach, I am ready to do such a contribution into the documentation after landing https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/155942 In this PR, Sample PGO documentation in Rustc was heavily reworked, and after merge I can add missing documentation pieces regarding Profi, FS-AFDO, etc.

We still be able to enable Profi or FS-AFDO (or anything else) by default in the future - this ability will stay with us anyway. Users's **default** experience shouldn't be a big issue for now since Sample PGO is has pretty limited usage across the Rust ecosystem nowadays. Even if Rustc behaviour will stay different from Clang's - we can fix it any time in the future.

What do you think about this way?

My issue with the trait split is that it's a lot of duplicated design (where to get some of the benefits of dyn-incompatibility, e.g. custom `AllocError`, we need entirely different methods on `DynAllocator` vs `Allocator`); my issue with having a blessed `DynAllocator` *type* is that we need to recreate the downcasting machinery by hand.

Ah, sorry, I was referring to a `trait DynAllocator` here. Yes, a `struct DynAllocatorBox` or similar would need this duplication. It would be even more if you want versions with and without `Send+Sync`.

The proposal above changed my mind on not having a dyn allocator trait. Given that we apparently can have both dyn-allocator and non-dyn-allocator, we probably should have both. body:
I do not think there is an "in the meantime" solution to this. There will have to be a decision between 
- `unsafe trait AllocatorClone: Allocator` (placeholder name)
    - Ugly, confusing
    -  Has analogous `AllocatorEq` solution for [#156917](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/156917)
- `unsafe trait AllocatorCloneMarker: Allocator + Clone` (placeholder name), similar to `TrustedLen`
    - Safety marker traits have historically been used only privately.
    -  Has analogous `AllocatorEqMarker` solution for [#156917](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/156917)
- (Permanent) `dyn`-incompatibility 
    - Inconvenient, requires custom `DynAllocator(dyn WrapperTrait)` that does not work with unsize cercions to get around
    - Still uses safe traits in safety requirements and is thus vulnerable to future language changes
    - Also solves [#156917](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/156917)
- Removing the impl for `Box` 
    - Makes `dyn Allocator` less useful because we cannot use `Container<T, Box<dyn Allocator>>`. However `Arc` still works and has strictly more API than `Box`
    - Still uses safe traits in safety requirements and is thus vulnerable to future language changes
    - Does not solve [#156917](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/156917) at all, which may still require seperate trait.
- Banning `impl Clone for Box<dyn Trait>`
    - Still uses safe traits in safety requirements and is thus vulnerable to future language changes
        - e.g. in-place init must ban `Clone for dyn Trait` or cannot generalize the clone for `Box`
    - Potentially Breaking
    - Analogous solution for [#156917](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/156917) would be to ban `PartialEq for dyn Trait`

Note that any use of safe traits in safety requirements (which is the case for all but the first two options):
- Requires care to be taken around future specialization in std 
- Can cause unsoundness under relaxation of orphan rules, including but not limited to user-defined `#[fundamental]`-like types.
- May rely on other current rules implicitly, like "subtrait of `dyn`-incompat is `dyn`-incompat"

If I missed any potential solution or potential issues with solutions, please tell me and I will list them.

We discussed this in the @rust-lang/libs-api meeting today and decided we need input from lang (and cc @rust-lang/types as well if they have a better idea). We can do one of three things:

1. Somehow mark unsafe certain traits as depending on the impl of safe traits. This was my idea in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/156920#issuecomment-4543400201; the proposed syntax is hideous, but it can just be an unstable attribute for now. The point is to block writing `impl Clone for dyn Allocator` without `unsafe`.
2. Use unsafe marker traits à la `unsafe trait AllocatorClone: Allocator + Clone` and remove the semantic requirements on `Allocator` implementors. This is kind of ugly and would be trait explosion but does address the issue. libs-api disliked this option most of the three unless there is a nicer way to do it.
3. Just make `Allocator` dyn-incompatible. The downside here is that it makes us all sad given how many things we axed to preserve dyn compatibility, but at this point there is zero downside to making the error an associated type.
4. (edit, secret bonus option 4) Mess with what `#[fundamental]` means... yikes.

I'm still personally of the opinion that something like (1) is best since a lot of folks do want dyn allocators, but will settle for something else if it comes to it. There is also the option of merging as-is if default associated types can get stabilised as that would enable us to make the call later (and add an alias `type Error = AllocError` retroactively) but I'm not holding my breath for that.

body:
> This can be a std only hack, it says "Clone is unsafe to implement for a type, if this other trait is also implemented for a type"

What exactly does this mean for generic impls? Does it require unsafe any time the type *might* `impl Allocator`? That sounds like a massive breaking change.

> Is actually sound. It will mean that the Clone impl for Box becomes unsafe. We'll have to have unsafe impl<T: Clone> Clone for Box<T>, which has a safety comment "unsafe is required because Box also impls allocator, and that is potentially problematic but it's not because Box' Clone impl is correct". It requires that T: Clone is also correct. But that's fine, because T also impls Allocator, so T's Clone impl is already unsafe, discharging the safety requirements.

Your argument still assumes that there is no *other* `impl Clone` for this Box. There could be a type where `A: Allocator` and `A: !Clone` and `Box<A>: Clone`.

> This could totally be a post-mono error even. 

Uh... consider me not a fan.^^ This sounds more like papering over a problem than actually fixing it. And I am not even confident it fixes the problem. The moment you have two traits that want to say "if this type also implements Clone then [some contract concerning that impl]", the system breaks down, because the `unsafe impl Clone` can't even know which contracts it is supposed to uphold.

> It's already true that PartialEq needs to be right for hashmaps to work.

That's a completely different discussion. I don't think it is appropriate to mix in this kind of logic error with soundness concerns.

> it's already true that this safe trait can have pretty disastrous side effects if badly implemented.

We have a big red line in the sand that's called UB. It makes a qualitative difference whether you can cross that line. So I don't think the situation is at all comparable.

I think it's just fundamentally a flawed argument to talk about "the Clone impl for this type" if you don't know whether the impl even exists.  The only ways to satisfy such an unsafe requirement are
- by knowing the impl so that we can point at it and say that it upholds the contract
- by knowing a negative impl which ensures that there can never be a clone that violates the contract

Traits are fundamentally an open-world concept, so trying to shoehorn closed-world reasoning into it is not going to go well. Explicit marker traits are the way to go IMO.

body: Impl-wise, this is "basically" just a way to autogenerate unsafe traits. `#[unsafe(has_preconditions(A))] trait B {}` is isomorphic to a macro that expands to `unsafe trait Unsafe_A_and_B {} trait B{}`; `#[unsafe(satisfies_preconditions(A))] impl<T: Whatever> B for T {}` expands to also `unsafe impl<T: Whatever> Unsafe_A_and_B for T {}`. ~~I disagree. In fact I'd argue the opposite is true. Allocators can implement clone to use the same memory pool or create a new one, so the set of allocators that can be cloned actually becomes larger. For example, an owning allocator type `A` can create a new memory pool on clone, which allows `Vec<T, A>` to be cloned (since `Vec::clone` doesn't care about the memory pool).~~

~~The only exception I can think of is something like `struct S<T, A: Allocator>(Arc<T, A>)`, which will not be able to derive `Clone` because `derive` is dumb with generics.~~

body:
To fix my previous comment:

I don't think it's that bad, since it only affects types that need the extra bound to be cloned. You can still implement `Clone` on allocators to return a fresh memory pool or the same one, so only types like `struct S<T, A: Allocator>(Arc<T, A>)` would be affected by `derive` using an overly strong bound for `A`.

body:
I've taken a closer look:
`lld` currently  [errors when given  LLVM bitcode for the nvptx target](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/3398f4e66558c67f7a8db70982d8bdbd8ed9a52d/lld/ELF/InputFiles.cpp#L1788). Therefore, I was unable to use `lld` for nvptx.

However, we could use the _internal fat lto functionality of rustc_ (the one used when `-Clto=fat` is specified). What it does is actually very similar to what llbc does: First, it links all necessary bitcode into a single module, which is then codegened.

Due to `obj_is_bitcode` being set for nvptx by default only bitcode is emitted in this final codegen step. However, with a small hack, I was able to make rustc always emit assembly after fat lto and produce a ptx file with no invokation of `llbc`.
I'm not sure if this is what we want, but I think it could work.

### Emitting PTX

From the discussion above it seems like emitting ptx is a missing piece of the puzzle.

### Handling libdevice

It's possible to hackily [link libdevice](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/libdevice-users-guide/basic-usage.html#linking-with-libdevice) using `llvm-bitcode-linker`. With LTO it works out really nicely. I don't think it will be an issue, but we need to make sure some way to continue linking to libdevice is preserved.

### Correctly handling `Linker::export_symbol`

A bloated .ptx file can cause problems as it's processed by the runtime. To let Rust nvptx users mitigate these problems we need to be able to only expose the public symbols from the library that is being built, which corresponds to the symbols listed by `Linker::export_symbol`. 

For `llvm-bitcode-linker` this is currently the default, and should continue to be so (at least in release mode).

### Other missing things

When rust-lld can provide us with the same features as llvm-bitcode-linker we should of course switch over. What about editing this issue into an unnumbered checklist with things to fix/remember in order to enable LLD for nvptx (and later phase out the llbc linker).

body:
I gave it a second try and was able to make lld work with nvptx. The necessary changes to plumb it together are very straightforward: [llvm](https://github.com/kulst/llvm-project/commit/711d31043d1a851f5d571182e4cede2486c1bd16), [rustc](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/fa726d4ce51c0cc79855b116be9f0b0637303b42). To produce a ptx file I use the following invocation: ` cargo +mybuild rustc --release -Zbuild-std=core -- -Ctarget-cpu=sm_80 -Clinker-plugin-lto -Clink-arg=--lto-emit-asm -Clink-arg=--plugin-opt=-mcpu=sm_80 -Clink-arg=--plugin-opt=-mattr=+ptx70 -Clink-arg=--plugin-opt=-addrsig=0 `
Cargo.toml 

[package]
name = "kernels"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
[lib]
name = "kernels"
path = "src/lib.rs"
crate-type = ["cdylib"]
[profile.release]
lto = true

.cargo/config.toml 

[build]
target = "nvptx64-nvidia-cuda"

The relevant option is `--lto-emit-asm`, which prevents `lld` from trying to emit an object file but instead assembly after lto happened. I found that `lld` just passes through the specified `--plugin-opt=-mcpu=sm_80` and `--plugin-opt=-mattr=+ptx70` to the final codegen. However, it does not do this for `-addrsig=0` (without my patch lld sets `addrsig` to true, which in turn results in an `.addrsig` section in the final ptx; ptxas complains about it). I do like this approach much more even though it makes small changes in lld necessary. By leveraging lld we can leave linking of arbitrary bitcode files (like libdevice) to it. If we use rustc's internal fat LTO we would have to read such arbitrary files. I was already able to verify that by using this approach it is easy to link against libdevice. With `-Lall=/usr/local/cuda/nvvm/libdevice` for example the following works: ```Rust #[link(name = "libdevice.10.bc", modifiers = "+verbatim")] unsafe extern "C" { unsafe fn __nv_umulhi(_a: u32, _b: u32) -> u32; } ``` There are still some small warnings by lld about `.rmeta` files which are neither `ET_REL` nor `LLVM bitcode`. But in general I think the approach works out nicely.

body:
I now have a [working prototype](https://github.com/kulst/rust/tree/nvptx-lld) that I am quite happy with. Since changes to LLVM are necessary for it to work, I haven't opened a pull request yet. However, I have opened the two PRs ([#200678](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/200678) and [#200679](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/200679)) to implement these changes in upstream LLVM.

With my protype, lld can be used for nvptx by specifying `-Clinker-flavor=ld.lld` and  `-Clinker=rust-lld`. 
A full invocation could therefore look like this: `cargo +mybuild rustc --target=nvptx64-nvidia-cuda -Zbuild-std=core --release -- -Ctarget-cpu=sm_80 -Clinker-flavor=ld.lld -Clinker=rust-lld`
To compile the necessary llvm components `llvm.download-ci-llvm = false` and `rust.lld = true` need to be set in your `bootstrap.toml`.

I would appreciate any feedback, especially if you encounter problems using it.

I would suggest that whenever the reference is bumped in rust-lang/rust, the PR containing these changes is tagged relnotes and then you can edit the auto-created issue with relevant context. That should ensure it gets picked up by the tooling and milestoned for the right release (once the relnotes PR is merged). Editing the reference by itself doesn't (imo) commit us until that change rides the train to stable after such a submodule bump.

https://forge.rust-lang.org/release/release-notes.html documents the relnotes process in more detail.
author: Mark-Simulacrum

body:
Thanks.  I worry, in practice, that we'll miss these without tooling support.  We reliably bump the submodule pointer for the books ahead of each beta bump (and, between those, at other intervals).  But we don't have a system for working backward from this to find everything that should be in the release notes when doing these mechanical bumps.

> https://forge.rust-lang.org/release/release-notes.html documents the relnotes process in more detail.

In that document, it notes:

> Once labeled, a new issue is automatically filed with title “Tracking issue for release notes of #xxxx: $original pr title”...
>
> Note that this step happens **on labeling**, not necessarily when the issue/PR is merged/closed.

In the Reference, I'd expect us to add these labels when merging.  Then, since we reliably update the submodule pointer ahead of the beta bump, it should be roughly predictable in which release the item will land.

Would it make any sense to extend this create-relnotes-tracking-issue-on-labeling behavior to the Reference repo as well?  (I imagine these tracking issues would live in `rust-lang/rust`.)
author: traviscross

body:
Hm, I see. I missed that a good portion of this is already automated (in particular file the book update PR), which I think makes it simpler to get this right.

Someone would need to:

1. Adjust the [relnotes handler](https://github.com/rust-lang/triagebot/blob/5f2081f6cf2782ca4936baad5a922c701201bf9c/src/handlers/relnotes.rs#L39) to cut rust-lang/rust tracking issues when the reference PR is tagged "relnotes" (or FCP).
2. Adjust the [milestone PRs](https://github.com/rust-lang/triagebot/blob/5f2081f6cf2782ca4936baad5a922c701201bf9c/src/handlers/milestone_prs.rs#L60-L73) handler to also milestone reference PRs. We seem to already do this for Cargo -- I'm not sure how reliable it is, the GitHub search seems broken for [no:milestone PRs](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Amerged+no%3Amilestone), but assuming that works it's a few lines of change to get that working.
3. Adjust the [relnotes handler](https://github.com/rust-lang/triagebot/blob/5f2081f6cf2782ca4936baad5a922c701201bf9c/src/handlers/relnotes.rs#L52-L64) to set the milestone on the rust-lang/rust tracking issue when the reference PR is milestoned. That might happen without any changes -- not entirely sure based on the code.
4. Update the [relnotes tool](https://github.com/rust-lang/relnotes/blob/master/src/main.rs) to properly handle tracking issues where the PR is on a different repository. I'm not sure how easy that will be, maybe it's a case of extending https://github.com/rust-lang/relnotes/blob/0892147a9519a56cc156924e8f33451656dc4f1b/src/main.rs#L98? But it may prove harder. The issue <> PR mapping is pretty hard to follow in that code, I always get confused when reading it.

@BoxyUwU has been tweaking the release note generation tooling I think, so may have alternative ideas. I think in principle that tooling *could* do the process above and scan rust-lang/reference and/or support rust-lang/rust tracking issues pointing at the reference, but I think we still need 90% of the above implemented since milestoning those tracking issues is otherwise difficult.

body:
> When the destructor of a `repr(packed)` struct runs, if it has a field which is unaligned and has a destructor, that field will be moved to an aligned place before the destructor of that field is ran. (See also [#143411](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/143411), [taiki-e/pin-project-lite#89](https://github.com/taiki-e/pin-project-lite/issues/89), [taiki-e/pin-project#34](https://github.com/taiki-e/pin-project/pull/34).)
> 
> The `#[pin_v2]` attribute does not take this into account. This allows a `Drop` impl of a type to access a value of that type via `&mut`, even after pin-projection was used to access a value of that same type via `Pin<&mut>`.
> 
> The below code demonstrates this unsoundness. The two addresses it prints are different, showing that the invariant of `Pin` was violated.
> 
> #![feature(pin_ergonomics)]
> #![expect(incomplete_features)]
> 
> use std::{
>     marker::PhantomPinned,
>     pin::{Pin, pin},
> };
> 
> #[pin_v2]
> #[repr(C, packed(4))]
> struct One<T>(T);
> 
> #[pin_v2]
> #[repr(C, align(65536))]
> struct Two(Thing);
> 
> struct Thing(#[expect(dead_code)] i32, PhantomPinned);
> 
> fn main() {
>     let pinned_one: Pin<&mut One<Two>> = pin!(One(Two(Thing(0, PhantomPinned))));
>     let &pin mut One(Two(ref pin mut pinned_thing)) = pinned_one;
>     access(pinned_thing);
> }
> 
> fn access(x: Pin<&mut Thing>) {
>     println!("Pinned access at {x:p}")
> }
> 
> impl Drop for Thing {
>     fn drop(&mut self) {
>         println!("Dropped at {self:p}");
>     }
> }
> Here's an explanation of the various parts this code:
> 
> * The `One` struct is packed to an alignment of 4 bytes. This causes the `Thing` field to also be aligned to 4 bytes, which allows projecting `pinned_one` to `pinned_thing` without causing a compile error due to an unaligned reference to `Thing`.
> * The `Two` struct is aligned to more than 4 bytes. This means that, when the destructor of `One` is ran, it notices that its field has an alignment of 65536. Therefore, this `Two` field is moved to an aligned place before `Two`'s destructor is ran.
> * The `One` struct needs to be generic, to work around a compile error that prevents me from directly putting a `repr(align)` type inside a `repr(packed)` type.
> 
> ### Meta
> Reproducible on the playground with version `1.98.0-nightly (2026-05-26 d1fc603d1788cc3c0eeb)`


I took a look into and reached this:

The simplest fix here is probably to just ban `#[pin_v2]` on `#[repr(packed)]`, which is what pin-project and pin-project-lite do. But I think that's broader than the actual hole, because a lot of this is already blocked today:

- E0588 ("packed type cannot transitively contain a `#[repr(align)]` type") already stops you from putting a concrete over-aligned field in a packed struct.
- `unaligned_references` (a hard error since #82523) already stops you from taking a reference to an under-aligned packed field.

So we can't drop a concrete `repr(align)` field in there, and you can't `&pin mut` an under-aligned leaf either.

But the real problem is the move-on-drop. When a `packed(N)` struct drops, any direct field `f` with `align(f) > N` gets moved to an aligned spot first, and that move takes whatever is inside `f` with it, including a deeper leaf that is fine on its own and was handed out as `Pin<&mut leaf>`. That's exactly what the repro does: `Thing` (align 4) is fine under `packed(4)`, so `unaligned_references` doesn't complain, but the field that moves is its parent `Two` (align 65536), and we never take a reference to `Two`, so nothing catches it.

So there are really two cases the current checks miss. The first is a generic field, like `One<T>`. We don't know `align(T)` at definition time, and it can go over `N` once it's monomorphized, which is the repro. The second is plain natural over-alignment, no generics needed: a `packed(4)` field whose natural alignment is 8 (it has a `u64` in it), with a pinned leaf at a 4-aligned offset. E0588 only checks `repr(align)`, not natural alignment, so this one slips through.

The generic one is the hard part, and honestly I don't think it can be both sound and permissive. `#[repr(packed(N))] #[pin_v2] struct One<T>(T)` is unsound the moment `T` has `align > N`, and there's no way to write "T's alignment is at most N" as a bound. So we have to restrict generic packed pin_v2 fields somehow no matter what.

That said, instead of banning the whole thing, what if we did a per-field check at the struct definition? Reject a `#[pin_v2]` `packed(N)` struct only when a field can have `align > N`: a generic field we can't prove, so reject it; a concrete field we just work out its alignment and compare. The rule is basically "a pin_v2 type has to promise none of its pinned fields ever get moved by drop glue", which under packing just means `align(field) <= pack` at every packed level. The good thing is the safe case still compiles (a `packed(N)` pin_v2 struct where every field is `<= N`), and both cases above are closed.

We could go further and check at the projection site instead, which would let `One<T>` stay defined and only reject the W-aligned uses. But that needs layout info right at the projection, and then you run into typeck running before layout, plus the post-mono cases, which feels like a lot of extra work for an experimental feature.

I'm leaning towards the per-field check, since the plain ban throws away cases that are actually fine. But I don't feel strongly about it, and the ban is obviously less risky to implement. I can put up a PR for whichever you'd rather have


What you think about it, @theemathas?

body:
> [@Dnreikronos](https://github.com/Dnreikronos) I worry that doing any logic involving alignment of types might cause a semver hazard.
> 
> That is, an upstream crate might define a type. A downstream crate then puts that type into a `#[pin_v2] #[repr(packed)]` struct. Later, the upstream crate updates private fields in that type, which increases the alignment. This causes the downstream crate to break. This happens even though it might not be obvious to the downstream crate's author that they're relying on the alignment of the upstream crate's type.
> 
> Therefore, I'm in favor of just banning `#[pin_v2]` on a `#[repr(packed)]` type. I doubt this would affect many use cases anyway.

Yeah, good observation on the semver hazard. That pretty much kills the per-field check for me. If compiling depends on a type's alignment, then an upstream crate bumping its alignment in a patch release would quietly break downstream code, and alignment was never something you're supposed to rely on anyway.
I can put up a PR for it, unless someone on the lang or compiler side wants to take it a different way.

body:
Hey @theemathas, ok so I studied this a bit more, here's where I'm at.

The main thing I missed before: the per-field align check (the idea where we'd only reject a packed pin_v2 struct if some field's align could go over the pack) doesn't actually save the repro at all. `One<T>` is generic, so there's no way to prove `align(T) <= N` at definition time, which means we'd end up rejecting it anyway. So that check would really only keep the narrow case alive where the struct is fully concrete and every field is already align <= N. That's a pretty niche set tbh, and we'd be paying for it with alignment-dependent compilation (the semver thing you mentioned), so imo not really worth it.

The only thing that would actually keep `One<T>` compiling is checking at the projection site instead of at the definition. But that one needs layout info right where the projection happens, and typeck runs before layout, plus the post-mono cases... it's a fair bit of work for an experimental feature and idk if it's worth doing right now.

So yeah, I'm leaning back towards just banning `#[pin_v2]` on `#[repr(packed)]`, like pin-project does (pin-project-lite too, though it leans on a lint trick that has a known align-1 hole, see taiki-e/pin-project-lite#89). It's sound, it's tiny to implement (basically a flag check next to the existing packed checks, no align logic at all, so no new semver hazard), and the part I like is that it doesn't lock us in: if we ever want the permissive projection-site version later, that one only ever *accepts more* code, so adding it wouldn't break anyone.

Lmk what you think. If you're good with the ban I'll put up a PR for it.

body:
Hi @GuillaumeGomez, I see you're assigned here. I looked into this one and have a fix ready, so I wanted to check with you before opening a PR in case you're already on it.

The panic is in `clean_fn_decl_with_params` (`src/librustdoc/clean/mod.rs`). It sugars the async return type whenever the fn header is async:

```rust
if let Some(header) = header && header.is_async() {
    output = output.sugared_async_return_type();
}
```

For a delegated async fn (`reuse Trait::foo`), the return type is `InferDelegation`, which `clean_ty` lowers to `Type::Infer`. That isn't the `impl Future<Output = ...>` shape `sugared_async_return_type` expects, so it hits the `else` and panics.

The sibling `clean_poly_fn_sig` already guards the same call with `if let Type::ImplTrait(_) = output`; the HIR path just doesn't. Adding that guard clears the ICE for every async delegation shape I tried (unit and non-unit returns, both at module level and inside an impl). I've got a `check-pass` regression test, and the full `rustdoc-ui` suite still passes.

One thing I left alone on purpose: rustdoc renders delegated fns with inferred types, like `pub async fn unit<Self>(self: _) -> _`. That's pre-existing and not specific to async. Plain sync delegation prints the same thing (`pub fn sync_unit<Self>(self: _) -> _`), since every delegation type cleans to `Infer`. Feels like a separate issue from the ICE, so I left it out. Happy to file it if it isn't tracked already.

If you haven't started on this, I'm glad to send the PR. If you've already got it in hand, no worries, I'll leave it with you.

body:
I looked into it briefly just now; here are some of my thoughts:

----

If you replace `type Next = Thing<Option<T>>;` with `type Next = Thing<T>;` you can actually get a reasonable error (on old versions/debug):

```
error[E0391]: cycle detected when computing layout of `Thing<i32>`
  --> src/main.rs:11:1
   |
11 | struct Thing<T: Chain>(T::Next, PhantomData<T>);
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
note: ...which requires computing layout of `<i32 as Chain>::Next`...
  --> src/main.rs:4:5
   |
 4 |     type Next;
   |     ^^^^^^^^^
   = note: ...which again requires computing layout of `Thing<i32>`, completing the cycle
   = note: see https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/overview.html#queries and https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/query.html for more information
```

---

The reason that the error is optimization level dependent is that the `layout_of` that triggers the error happens in codegen. If mir opts remove the code before it goes to codegen, there are no calls to `layout_of` and thus no error.

---

It's a bit weird that we disallow

```rust
struct X(X);
```
saying "`error[E0072]: recursive type `X` has infinite size`". Nothing is stopping us from making `X` have finite size (`0`) (this is not very useful as it only works for zsts, but maybe the error should be tweaked for this case).

---

Depending on `layout_of` being called in random places (like the code I changed in #150447) seems fragile. If we truly wanted to disallow infinitely recursive types, we should probably either check for them explicitly, or call `layout_of` on all types explicitly (both of which probably result in perf loss...)

Yeah, at the moment V8+ is unimplemented in LLVM aside from toggling the ELF bits...

> So seems like different targets use different ABIs here. Is v9 yet another different ABI?

V9 is an ISA level, it adds CAS and a couple other instructions.
At least in upstream (and GCC) using it implies using V8+ ABI by default, since most of the addition to the ISA operates on the full 64-bit registers anyway, so turning off V8+ doesn't make much sense at V9 ISA level (edit: but is technically possible e.g. by passing `-mcpu=v9 -mno-v8plus` in GCC or clang).

body: SPARC V9 has 64-bit registers (and new instructions), SPARC V8 has 32-bit registers. SPARC V8+ is 32-bit code running on a SPARC V9 system (so can use the new instructions).

body:
> Should our targets use V8 or V8+?

[Linux](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.94.0/compiler/rustc_target/src/spec/targets/sparc_unknown_linux_gnu.rs#L18) and [Solaris (unsupported in rustc)](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/llvmorg-22.1.0/clang/lib/Driver/ToolChains/Arch/Sparc.cpp#L170) use V8+, others use V8 AFAIK.

> That sounds a bit like `x32`... except that is a variant of the 64bit target (`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnux32`) whereas apparently V8+ is a variant of the 32bit target?

Yeah, in my understanding, x32 is a variant of the x86_64 64-bit ABI that changes pointer size, system call numbers, etc., but v8plus is a variant of sparc32 ABI that adds and extends several registers and instructions. IMO the former is more powerful because it can supports full 64-bit ISA, but it causes more problems because code that assumes pointer size based on the architecture does not work properly.

So I think we have essentially two levers to fix this. ## Forbid the clone The first option is to somehow make `Pin>` only implement `Clone` if `A: 'static`. One way could be a new trait like this: ```rs trait PinClone: Clone { fn pin_clone(self: &Pin) -> Pin; } impl Clone for Pin

{} impl Copy for Pin

This approach may also be able to fix #134407. I personally believe the most with the second option, but I do think we should try a crater run for the first approach to see how bad it would be before making a decision.

This is an intentional compiler change, done in #155473 (cc @scottmcm, author of the PR). The compiler now uses `-1` instead of `5` to represent `None` in this case. This results in more performant programs in some cases.

Other than the cases [listed in the documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/index.html#representation), which value is used to represent `None` is *not* a stable guarantee. body:
I dug into this. The root cause is in how a braced const argument is lowered under `min_generic_const_args`.

`FieldName<{ FieldName::len() }>` lowers the braced `FieldName::len()` to `ConstArgKind::TupleCall`, because AST lowering treats any `path(args)` call expression in const-arg position as a tuple constructor. Then `lower_const_arg_tuple_call` lowers the callee's `Self` type, `FieldName`, which was written without its `const N: usize` argument. That bare type is what triggers the "missing generics" (E0107) cascade. But `FieldName::len()` is an associated-function call, not a constructor, so treating it as a `TupleCall` is wrong to begin with.

That leaves a design question I'd like to confirm before sending a PR: how should mgca treat a braced, non-constructor call in const-arg position?

(a) Reject it and require `const { ... }`, reusing the "complex const arguments must be placed inside of a `const` block" diagnostic that AST lowering already emits for other complex expressions. tracing's macro expansion would then need to wrap the call in `const { }`.

(b) Accept the bare braces (fall back to an anon const), so it keeps compiling the way it did before the feature was enabled.

I have (a) implemented: detect the non-constructor self type before lowering it, then emit the const-block diagnostic. Happy to open that PR, but if (b) is the intended behavior the fix looks quite different, so I'd rather confirm the direction first.

Could whoever owns the mgca work say which behavior is intended?

This one is a braced *call* (`{ FieldName::len() }`) that gets lowered as a tuple constructor when it's actually an associated function. Different code paths, so they'll need separate fixes even though both trace back to mgca rejecting code that built fine before the flag was on. body:
So, the change that initially forced the retention of the frame pointer was introduced in [c9b87ac](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/c9b87ac4b306cf43ca6e46defb91267fe257e45b). Based on the comments, it was originally intended to prevent the LR register from being corrupted in `nounwind` (later changed to `noreturn`) functions. However, at that time, the option appeared to exempt leaf functions (or perhaps required an additional option).

The upgrade from Rust 1.86.0 to 1.87.0 brought LLVM 20, where this behavior changed: LLVM 20 now requires the explicit -momit-leaf-frame-pointer option to continue exempting leaf functions.

Initially, this setting was specific to M-profile targets, but later the thumb configuration was apparently promoted to a common default for all arm-none-* targets, which extended the change to A- and R-profile targets as well. That likely explains the regression between 1.94.0 and 1.95.0.

So the question is: was retaining the frame pointer in leaf functions part of the original intent? Should there be an option to allow specific functions to continue omitting the frame pointer?

body:
Hey @theemathas and @JonathanBrouwer  I've implemented a fix for this issue and have a PR open.

**What I did:**
Added `check_path_attribute` validation in `rustc_passes/src/check_attr.rs` that catches the four cases for `#[path]` / `#![path]` misuse:

- **Case 1 (error):** `#[path]` on an inline module with no external submodules - the attribute is meaningless since the compiler already knows where the inline body is.
- **Case 2 (valid):** `#[path]` on an external module (`mod x;`) or an inline module that *does* have external submodules - this is the legitimate use-case.
- **Case 3 (valid):** `#![path]` inside a module that has at least one external submodule -meaningful as a directory hint.
- **Case 4 (error):** `#![path]` inside a module with no external submodules - useless since there are no external files to locate.

I also added a UI test (`tests/ui/attributes/path-inline-module.rs`) with 5 error cases covering all the nonsensical patterns. All tests pass with `--stage 1 --bless`.

Let me know if you have feedback on the approach or the error messages!

the implementation handles this case correctly - the following will **not** produce a warning:

```rust
mod thread {
    #![path = "thread_files"]
    #[path = "tls.rs"]
    mod local_data;
}
```

Since `local_data` is an external module (`mod local_data;` with no body), `has_nested_external_modules` returns `true`, so the `#![path]` inner attribute is treated as meaningful and no error is emitted.

 I'm actively working on this - have an implementation with passing tests ready and opened a PR. Happy to share the approach for review!

body:
I was able to reproduce this locally, and I believe  it's the same underlying bug raised on #25860 (implied bounds + variance), specifically the higher-ranked case. Linking the two so they don't get lost.

What is found was #129021 added a well-formedness check on the reified fn pointer in borrowck, and that already rejects the non-higher-ranked forms. For example, this one errors now:

```rust
let f: fn(_, &'a T) -> &'static T = foo;  // error: 'a must outlive 'static
```

The interesting part is that the same PR knew the higher-ranked case was still open: it added a `known-bug: #25860` test at `tests/ui/implied-bounds/implied-bounds-on-nested-references-plus-variance-2.rs`, and its own comment in `rustc_borrowck::type_check` says the check "only works when we're casting to a non-higher-ranked fn ptr."

The case raised here it's exactly that same problem. The elided reference makes the target fn pointer higher-ranked, and it sails right through:

```rust
let f: fn(_, &T) -> &'static T = foo;     // still compiles
```

The reason it compiles: the implied bound the call relies on ends up under the `for<>` binder, and fn-pointer WF doesn't track it there. wf.rs even has a long-standing comment about this exact thing, already pointing at #25860: "there is no way for us to express a fn type complete with the implied bounds that it is assuming."

So I think this is the higher-ranked residual of #25860. I would like to have an opinion from the T-types folks about the decision whether to keep this issue as the tracked minimal repro for that form or fold it into #25860.
author: Dnreikronos

body:
Agreed the main root cause is issue-25860, the repro is nearly identical to the testcase as I mentioned.

But I don't think this is simply the 25860 bug resurfacing. The similar testcase has compiled at least as far back as I tested (2018), whereas this shape only started compiling at pr-72493 (2020-06, the leak-check move). So despite looking the same, this form was rejected for years until it was newly exposed.

Even if this folds into 25860, that pr-72493 regression point seems worth recording.

body:
> Agreed the main root cause is issue-25860, the repro is nearly identical to the testcase as I mentioned.
> 
> But I don't think this is simply the 25860 bug resurfacing. The similar testcase has compiled at least as far back as I tested (2018), whereas this shape only started compiling at pr-72493 (2020-06, the leak-check move). So despite looking the same, this form was rejected for years until it was newly exposed.
> 
> Even if this folds into 25860, that pr-72493 regression point seems worth recording.

Yeah, make sense!
Seems like that the `-2.rs` shape has been broken for some time already(years), but this higher-ranked form was actually rejected until #72493 (the leak-check move) in 2020, so it's a real regression, not something that was always compiling.

I separated like this: #25860 is the underlying logical hole (implied bounds + variance + fn-pointer coercion). The old leak check seems to have been guarding this particular higher-ranked coercion by accident. Before #72493 it failed with `error[E0308]: ... expected concrete lifetime, found bound lifetime parameter`. #72493 moved the leak check out of higher-ranked subtyping and into coherence and candidate evaluation, and that removed the incidental guard, which is what exposed this form.

I believe that the right approach would look like this: probably we shouldn't  revert of #72493. The leak check was only catching this by accident, and #72493 moved it on purpose. The fix #25860 has always needed is the right one here too: make fn-pointer well-formedness track the implied bound under the `for<>` binder, so the coercion gets rejected on WF grounds instead of incidentally by the leak check.

So two facts, both worth keeping. The root cause is the #25860 family. This specific form is a #72493 regression that was correctly rejected for years. The regression isn't a footnote to the root cause, and I agree it should be recorded whether or not the issue ends up folded.


What you think, @cushionbadak?

Personally I think that removing prioritize is fine, because I don't think "this works perfectly fine but the assembly is less nice" qualifies for tracking as a "regression" in any meaningful way.

> Within the optimization pipeline, I noticed that the LLVM IR was the same up until the `X86 DAG->DAG Instruction Selection (x86-isel)` step.

That says to me that this isn't anything to do with Rust, and should be filed to LLVM instead, since it's what handles `isel`.

The MIR is completely fine <https://rust.godbolt.org/z/ovsEenh1j>, with the closures inlined and such, down to just the obvious 4 basic blocks.  There's no "add on maybe-uninitialized" construct in MIR, so it can't be branchless in MIR.
author: scottmcm

body:
For reference, this IR is:
```llvm
define void @f(ptr noalias noundef align 4 captures(none) dereferenceable(8) %x) unnamed_addr #0 {
start:
  %0 = load i32, ptr %x, align 4
  %1 = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %x, i64 4
  %2 = trunc nuw i32 %0 to i1
  %3 = load i32, ptr %1, align 4
  %_5 = add i32 %3, 1
  %y.sroa.5.0 = select i1 %2, i32 %_5, i32 undef
  store i32 %y.sroa.5.0, ptr %1, align 4
  ret void
}
```

Based on the select undef in the input, this is probably related to correctness fixes for poison propagation.

You can see the `freeze` in the SDAG dump:
```
Optimized legalized selection DAG: %bb.0 'f:start'
SelectionDAG has 13 nodes:

        t21: i32 = freeze t9
```

body:
Here's the difference in the IR in nightly today as we give it to LLVM: <https://rust.godbolt.org/z/zzEWqrxa3>

```llvm
define void @can_alias(ptr noundef %x) unnamed_addr {
start:
  %0 = load i32, ptr %x, align 4
  %1 = add i32 %0, 1
  store i32 %1, ptr %x, align 4
  call void @fancy()
  %2 = load i32, ptr %x, align 4
  %3 = add i32 %2, 1
  store i32 %3, ptr %x, align 4
  ret void
}

define void @noalias(ptr noalias noundef align 4 dereferenceable(4) %x) unnamed_addr {
start:
  %0 = load i32, ptr %x, align 4
  %1 = add i32 %0, 1
  store i32 %1, ptr %x, align 4
  call void @fancy()
  %2 = load i32, ptr %x, align 4
  %3 = add i32 %2, 1
  store i32 %3, ptr %x, align 4
  ret void
}

declare void @fancy() unnamed_addr #0
``` 

There's nothing for rust to do differently here.

If you're unhappy with the instruction selection LLVM is doing from that <https://llvm.godbolt.org/z/999G7Gr9T>, then you probably want to report it to them: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/new/choose

There are diagnostic issues with reusing the name `Vec`, even if it's in a different module. Usually `std::vec::Vec` is trimmed to just `Vec` when it appears in suggestions and other diagnostics. However, if there's another type called `Vec` then this doesn't happen.

```diff
 	   |         ^ expected `&[_; 0]`, found `&Vec<u8>`
 	   |
 	   = note: expected reference `&[_; 0]`
-	              found reference `&Vec<u8>`
+	              found reference `&std::vec::Vec<u8>`
 ```

Rustdoc also has an issue where `fallible::Vec` will be shortened to just `Vec`, which is especially confusing in the `vec::Vec` docs.

I tried renaming it to `FallibleVec` for the sake of experimentation but this surfaced another diagnostic issue: `FallibleVec` is suggested above `Vec`. This is not great because `Vec` is definitely the type most people should reach for.

```diff
error[E0277]: can't compare `[{integer}; Self::HOST_SIZE]` with `[{integer}; 0]`
  --> $DIR/too_generic_eval_ice.rs:11:30
   |
LL |         [5; Self::HOST_SIZE] == [6; 0]
   |                              ^^ no implementation for `[{integer}; Self::HOST_SIZE] == [{integer}; 0]`
   |
   = help: the trait `PartialEq<[{integer}; 0]>` is not implemented for `[{integer}; Self::HOST_SIZE]`
   = help: the following other types implement trait `PartialEq<Rhs>`:
+             `&[T]` implements `PartialEq<FallibleVec<U, A>>`
             `&[T]` implements `PartialEq<Vec<U, A>>`
             `&[T]` implements `PartialEq<[U; N]>`
             `&[u8; N]` implements `PartialEq<ByteStr>`
             `&[u8; N]` implements `PartialEq<ByteString>`
             `&[u8]` implements `PartialEq<ByteStr>`
             `&[u8]` implements `PartialEq<ByteString>`
-             `&mut [T]` implements `PartialEq<Vec<U, A>>`
-             `&mut [T]` implements `PartialEq<[U; N]>`
-           and 11 others
+             `&mut [T]` implements `PartialEq<FallibleVec<U, A>>`
+           and 14 others
```

I guess what I'd want here is some way to deprioritise `fallible::Vec` in diagnostics so `vec::Vec` can be shortened and `fallible::Vec` is displayed later in suggestions (or not at all).

body:
I'm still trying to figure out what's going on.

What is clear:
- the `crate::prelude::*` import gets into `maybe_unused_trait_imports`, that's why it's reported as unused after type checking (compiler\rustc_hir_analysis\src\check_unused.rs), the imported *trait* is indeed not used
- import gets into `maybe_unused_trait_imports` because `/// [A::f]` forces collection of traits in scope (and imports to them), and their addition to the potentially unused trait import set

What is not clear:
- why the `crate::prelude::*` import is not *removed* from the `maybe_unused_trait_imports` set, which is typically happens with imports that are used early, before type checking
  - basically early unused import checking considers the import neither unused (otherwise it'd report it), nor used (otherwise it'd remove it from maybe_unused_trait_imports)

body:
This is an invalid implementation of `Ord`.  `PartialOrd` and `Ord` require transitivity.  The docs says:
> Violating these requirements is a logic error. The behavior resulting from a logic error is not specified, but users of the trait must ensure that such logic errors do not result in undefined behavior.

`BTreeSet` as a consumer of `Ord` is allowed to have unspecified behavior (including panic) when a type misimplements `Ord`.  I don't believe that there is a coherent ordering for `BTreeMap` to use in this case, and it was probably previously depending on internal details about iteration order and insertion.

I don't believe this should be considered a regression, unless there's a large amount of ecosystem breakage for some weird reason.

author: jmsperu

body:
**Where it originates: MIR drop elaboration emits an `O(N²)` cleanup ladder, before LLVM runs.**

Counting basic blocks / `drop` terminators / cleanup blocks in the optimized MIR of `build()` (`rustc 1.94.1 -O --emit=mir`):

| N | variant | bbs | `drop`s | cleanup bbs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | baseline (interleaved `?`) | 321 | 254 | 269 |
| 16 | bind-then-build | 82 | 30 | 31 |
| 32 | baseline | 1153 | 1022 | 1053 |
| 32 | bind-then-build | 162 | 62 | 63 |
| 64 | baseline | 4353 | 4094 | 4157 |
| 64 | bind-then-build | 322 | 126 | 127 |

For the interleaved-divergence aggregate literal, MIR `drop` terminators and cleanup blocks are **≈ N²** (4094 ≈ 64² at N=64); the bind-then-build form is **≈ 2N**. Each construction point gets its own cleanup chain that drops the suffix of already-initialized elements, so the partially-initialized aggregate produces a quadratic cleanup ladder at the MIR level — already present before any LLVM pass runs. The ~`O(N³)` wall-clock is then the function-opt pipeline (`InstCombine`/`CorrelatedValuePropagation`/`JumpThreading`) running super-linearly on top of that `O(N²)` CFG.

So this looks like it's rooted in drop elaboration for partially-initialized aggregate literals, with LLVM's super-linearity compounding it. `python3 mir_count.py` in the repro repo reproduces the counts.

author: tomassedovic

body:
I think there's maybe a misunderstanding about what changed. For cargo, nothing changes since we added back the behavior in https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17110. Cargo's locking is always inter-process. The `fcntl` style locking differs in what happens for locks on separate handles within the same process. Cargo only ever uses a single handle per process, so it is not affected.

So, release-notes-wise, I don't think there's anything that needs to be said regarding cargo.

But thanks for circling back on it, I forgot to get back here.

body:
Yeah I do actually wonder whether it makes sense to scope these under `cfg(unix)`. Because then all users of them will either need to write explicitly platform specific code or give up non-`unix` support. I could easily see myself, for example, wanting to build a little tool or script for myself that uses XDG. I would much rather have it "just work" on Windows using XDG (even though it's inappropriate) than have it not work at all. And @programmerjake's point about Android is kind of the opposite problem.

I realize that _needing_ to write platform specific code in order to use XDG could be seen as a feature. Because it forces you to think about it and makes it harder to do the wrong thing in _some_ environments. But it also makes it harder to do the thing that will "just work" for some classes of programs where absolute correctness isn't needed. (Like how using `unwrap()` for error handling is sometimes okay and very useful.)

author: nia-e

body:
We talked about this extensively in today's @rust-lang/libs-api meeting.

@nia-e can follow-up with more details, but here's the rough sketch we wanted:

- This needs to handle failure, using `io::Result`, as well as things being missing, via `Option`.
- This should cache the results, and represent that as a struct. For instance, the `directories` crate provides a set of types like `UserDirs`, that in turn have methods returning `Option`.

So, we'd like to have have *portable* types (with private fields) for the set of directories, with methods on those types returning `Option<PathBuf>`, optionally target-specific extension traits for non-portable fields, and then target-specific functions to return (an `io::Result` of) the struct. That way, UNIX platforms can have a function to get the XDG version, macOS can have a function to get the macOS version (so macOS has both and users can decide), and so on.

We could also have a portable method that creates one with entirely `None` values, so that people can fill one in themselves.

Things we left open in the design:
- Should we have private fields with `set_` methods, or non-exhaustive public fields? The latter are easier to work with, but the former means we can add fields via target-specific extension traits.

@nia-e, did I forget anything?
author: joshtriplett

body:
That's a version of the API I can get behind, and I can commit to implementing it.

I would strongly lean towards the method interface. This means consumers can't take ownership of the individual path configuration directly, but the set of OS-provided well known directories is so disjoint between hosts that OS-specific extension traits seems like the only useful way to expose this that doesn't overload the OS-agnostic documentation with OS-specific information.

body:
You have to distinguish the interaction with `&mut`/`&` to the *outside* the `UnsafeCell` and with `&mut`/`&` to the *inside* the `UnsafeCell` .

For references to the outside, the docs mention both `&` and `&mut` extensively -- the latter mostly to explain that there are no interactions, `&mut UnsafeCell<T>` is basically the same as `&mut T`, you can *not* get out of the uniqueness of mutable references with an `UnsafeCell`.

For references to the inside, the only legal way to get a pointer to the "inside" is `get` (and `get_raw`). And then once you did that you can turn that raw pointer into a mutable reference or shared reference, whatever you need. We don't have special docs for either of these cases as far as I can tell? At this point "normal" raw pointer rules apply, nothing specific to `UnsafeCell`.

> the documentation covers the interactions of &mut and UnsafeCell very thoroughly

So IOW, I don't know which part of the docs you are referring to here. The only long paragraph about `&mut` is about *outside* references (and we discuss outside shared references as well, in fact most of the docs talk about that case), but your question seems to be about *inside* references.
author: RalfJung

body:
> For references to the inside, the only legal way to get a pointer to the "inside" is `get` (and `get_raw`). And then once you did that you can turn that raw pointer into a mutable reference or shared reference, whatever you need.

If the documentation contained the phrase “you can turn that … into a shared reference” that would be an improvement. As it is, when I scan the documentation, I find references to what I can *do* with an `&T` reference, but not how to create it:

> If you create a safe reference with lifetime 'a (either a &T or &mut T reference), then you must not access the data in any way that contradicts that reference for the remainder of 'a.

and I find references to creating an `&mut T` reference, but not an `&T` reference:

> Note that the only valid way to obtain a *mut T pointer to the contents of a shared UnsafeCell<T> is through .get() or .raw_get(). A &mut T reference can be obtained by either dereferencing this pointer or by calling .get_mut() on an exclusive UnsafeCell<T>.

but there is nothing that **states explicitly** that if I want an `&T` reference, I should be going through the `*mut T` (well, or calling the unstable `.as_ref_unchecked()`). It's *possible to draw this conclusion* by carefully reading the text and acting conservatively, but it's not *easy*. I think the documentation should make it *easy* to learn this fact.

This issue is not like a UCG issue where the main point is clarification of what the boundaries of sound code *are*; it is a request that the documentation be written to better introduce the reader to the space in which those boundaries are drawn, because it is not obvious.

body:
The one issue cited here and in my original issue field against `getrandom` that you cited is not the only issue with using `esp_fill_random`. The documentation doesn't provide enough information to make a determination of how the "Random Number Generator" box in the diagram in the documentation works. Is it really just the XOR of the input sources? Or does it do additional "mixing"?

If it doesn't do additional mixing, that definitely is that not good enough "mixing" to be considered a CSPRNG because the output would be non-uniform, and is likely leaking sensitive information from the input sources directly into its output.

If it does do additional "mixing," we can't assume anything about the quality of the mixing.

Either way, we have to assume the output is non-uniform *even given "enough entropy"*, to speak very loosely.

Contrast this with Intel's documentation about how RDRAND works, where the input sources are fed into a software DRBG conforming to NIST/ISO standards before being output. The same with Linux's CSPRNG and basically every operating system's API.

Another feature of most operating system APIs is the hedging against lack of entropy from the various entropy sources. If you look at how Linux or other OS entropy management is handled, it is quite complicated. Usually the user/application also has the ability to help with the entropy management.

In a sense, ESP-IDF isn't a full operating system; it seems to be designed with the expectation that the user will plug in their own CSPRNG that is seeded (in part) from `esp_fill_random`, using that CSPRNG instead of `esp_fill_random` directly, and mixing additional entropy sources into it.
author: briansmith

body:
(Take this with a huge grain of salt as I'm not a security expert. Critical feedback welcome!)

> In a sense, ESP-IDF isn't a full operating system; it seems to be designed with the expectation that the user will plug in their own CSPRNG that is seeded (in part) from `esp_fill_random`, using that CSPRNG instead of `esp_fill_random` directly, and mixing additional entropy sources into it.

I think so yes. `esp_(fill_)random` claims to be a TRNG (when the stars are properly aligned i.e. the Radio is on), but NOT a CSPRNG. I.e. one needs to layer on top chachaXX or similar, and use `esp_(fill_)random` as a seed.

This is how MbedTLS is configured in the ESP-IDF SDK - `esp_(fill_)random` is used as the (only) entropy source for [MbedTLS's CTR-DRBG CSPRNG](https://github.com/espressif/esp-idf/blob/master/components/mbedtls/port/esp_hardware.c).

(ESP-IDF is not an OS btw in the traditional sense, just a task scheduler + a bunch of POSIX-like libs, all running in "ring 0" as you don't have other rings on microcontrollers; the whole thing has ~ 300-500KB SRAM and then ~ 4MB NOR Flash where the code resides and is executed using XIP techniques.)

(
A deviation related to `getrandom`:

I must admit I find the whole situation with `getrandom` and `rand` a bit confusing, but then I do not really have any in-depth understanding of security.

Here's my confusion: given that `rand` anyway uses the bytes returned by `getrandom` just as an entropy seed for its chachaXX CSPRNG variant used by `thread_rng` (right?), why is it necessary in the first place for `getrandom` to be cryptographically secure (i.e. something stronger than just entropy)?
)

Regarding what should be used in the STD "rand" module itself when compiled against ESP-IDF:
The best we can do I guess is use `esp_fill_random` as an entropy source and then chachaXX (say - from `rand`)  as a CSPRNG.

Would STD's `random` module work on "OS"s that can only provide some entropy, and then STD would provide a CSPRNG on top, or are you expecting a true CSPRNG from the OS (a bit like `getrandom`)?

Judging by the comments [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/d2f24127d97d8c795d1cf5fbf6037f9885f34d39/library/std/src/sys/random/getentropy.rs#L1) it seems to be (unfortunately) the latter?

body:
It seems we had two different approved MCPs proposing essentially the same thing:
- MCP 950, proposing `-Z lint-rust-version`
- [MCP 772](https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-team/issues/772), proposing `--hint-msrv`.

Both went through essentially the same discussion over again: people identified that this shouldn't be used as anything more than a hint, and thus that got encoded in the name. For MCP 950, this changed it from `-Z msrv=...` to `-Z lint-rustc-version=...`. For MCP 772, this added "hint" to change it to `--hint-msrv`.

Proposal: could we consolidate these two, around the name `--hint-msrv`? Rationale:
- This is about the *minimum supported* Rust version (MSRV), and `rustc-version` doesn't specify "minimum supported".
- "hint" makes it semantically clearer that this should not be used for anything load-bearing.

body:
Invested some time on this a bit. the check that should catch it (`ProjectOnNonPinProjectType` in `pat.rs`) is gated on `pat.default_binding_modes`, so it only runs for the implicit projection. explicit `&pin mut` / `ref pin mut` go through `check_pat_ref` -> `check_pat_tuple_struct`/`check_pat_struct`, which dont do any pin or packed check at all (no `packed` anywhere in `pat.rs`).

so two things fall out, not just the packed bug: the hole here, and explicit projection skiping `#[pin_v2]` entirely. idk if that second ones a bug or intended (explicit = the manual path that doesn't need the attr?), and that kinda decides the fix. this compiles today, nothing packed, no `#[pin_v2]`:

```rust
#[repr(C)]
struct One<T>(T);
let &pin mut One(Two(ref pin mut x)) = pinned_one; // accepted
```

good thing is the signal's alredy there: `check_pat_ref` sets `pat_info.max_pinnedness = Pinned` after peeling `&pin mut`, and it flows down to every subpattern (the binding site already uses it for the `Unpin` bound). so the only new bit is `adt.repr().packed()`.

three ways imo:

(1) gate the explicit path on `#[pin_v2]` too, i.e. run `ProjectOnNonPinProjectType` there as well. #157542 (still open) bans `#[pin_v2]` + packed, so once that lands this closes the packed hole for free and makes explicit/implicit match. only works if the skip is a bug though.

(2) blunt packed check at the destructure:

```rust
if pat_info.max_pinnedness == PinnednessCap::Pinned
    && let ty::Adt(adt, _) = pat_ty.kind()
    && adt.repr().packed()
{ /* error: cannot pin-project through a #[repr(packed)] type */ }
```

same move as #157542 (ban the combo), matches the `upvar.rs` capture restriction that stops at a packed field regardless of alignment. one false positive: `&pin mut Packed(x)` by value is sound but gets rejected. rare, dont care.

(3) like 2 but precise: thread a "went through packed" flag on `PatInfo`, reset on deref (like `most_packed_projection`), error only when a pinned ref's actually formed. no false positives, just more fiddly.

leaning 2 to start, 3 later if the by-value case ever bites. but if explicit should just require `#[pin_v2]` like implicit, 1 is cleaner and i'll do that. ltk what you prefer.

cc @theemathas @mejrs

body: I think only approach 1 is the only viable approach, due to #157634.

A related case is the following code, where there is weirdness even with optimization turned off:

```rust
fn main() {
    std::hint::black_box(0 as *const [u64; 1 << 63]);
}
```

This program compiles and runs fine when compiled with `rustc main.rs` (no optimization and no debuginfo).

This program fails to compile with the following error when compiled with `rustc main.rs -Cdebuginfo=2`
```text
error: values of the type `[u64; 9223372036854775808]` are too big for the target architecture

error: aborting due to 1 previous error
```

And this program produces the following error when ran with miri:

```text
error: post-monomorphization error: values of the type `[u64; 9223372036854775808]` are too big for the target architecture
 --> src/main.rs:2:26
  |
2 |     std::hint::black_box(0 as *const [u64; 1 << 63]);
  |                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ post-monomorphization error occurred here
```
author: theemathas

body:
> This program compiles and runs fine when compiled with rustc main.rs (no optimization and no debuginfo).

That is surprising, I would not have expected us to skip computing the layout here.

My guess is that when we compute the layout of the raw pointer, we quickly determine that the pointee is sized, and then we don't look at the pointee any further.

For this specific case, the reason Miri raises that error is that we do actually create a place to the pointee when validating a raw pointer. We could consider avoiding this.

body:
I suspect this is caused by #142915 which enabled DestProp by default in 1.92. While this allows multiple `LargeStruct` locals to be merged, it also removes all storage statements (which are used to generated LLVM lifetime annotations) for the merged locals.

This is also partially caused by GVN since that pass causes the `[const 0_u8; 1024]` to be shared by the initializers of the 2 `LargeStruct`, which in turn means that the array's lifetime overlaps with the lifetime of `a`, requiring 2 separate stack slots.

author: nia-e

body:
For the wasm part of this specifically, yes, using a mutex *anywhere* is basically forbidden on the main thread in browsers. Personally I don't think it's reasonable to expect the standard library to use zero mutexes on wasm and make absolutely everything lock-free. This is a consequence of browsers and not something Rust can "just" fix. Basically I would not recommend changing the implementation and instead leaving it as-is. I'll note that there's a long and storied history of blocking-the-main-thread-with-wasm-threads in the browser, and I'm not putting in all the context here. 

For the documentation part, I'm not sure what the best outcome for wasm is. In practice virtually nothing in the standard library synchronization-wise, except maybe `Arc`, can be used on the main thread in wasm. @cyexclam I would caution you, for example, from using basically anything libstd/crates.io-based on the main thread of wasm. You basically have to hand-write everything to ensure the main thread *only* uses atomics/async and nothing else. AFAIK virtually none of the ecosystem is built for that so it's inevitably wasm-specific, and this is one of the primary reasons that threads-related wasm things are perma-stuck at tier 3.

---

One possible solution is to do what Emscripten did. As @Mark-Simulacrum a spin lock is the canonical fix for this. The malloc lock in the standard library already does this, and Emscripten uses spin locks on the main thread for all locks in wasm I believe. Robustly doing this would require detecting whether the current thread is the main thread, and the Rust standard library has no means of doing that. External JS embeddings can hook up something, but libstd has no means of checking. That would mean that this solution would be that locks on wasm are *always* spin locks for Rust, and I do not personally think that is an acceptable solution.

Basically everything here is between and a rock and a hard place. No solution is good, and I would recommend placing the burden on users of the threads-in-wasm target because, in my opinion, it's not worth inflicing the "weirdness" of the main thread on the rest of the library/ecosystem.
