body:
@jacobsa 

> That documentation is ambiguous about whether it means to say "this is the definition of ABI compatibility when used anywhere in the standard library ([example](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/f28ac764c36004fa6a6e098d15b4016a838c13c6/library/core/src/mem/maybe_uninit.rs#L214))", or just "this is what ABI compatibility means in the specific context of functions", particularly because it's in documentation specific to functions.

"ABI compatibility" is a term we specifically use for function calls. This is a language-level definition, not a library-level one, we just document it in the library. The docs are pretty clear about that IMO: any function call where caller and callee signature are *not* ABI-compatible is UB.

> The definition used there is much narrower than used in the rest of the world

That's like saying "x86 asm has less UB than Rust". That's both correct and expected. You seem to make the classic mistake of trying to do asm-level reasoning when thinking about a Rust program -- but that's [just not valid](https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2019/07/14/uninit.html).

Note that (function call) ABI compatibility in C and C++ is even narrower than what we have in Rust -- consult the respective standard for details. The document you cite is only relevant when writing asm; it does *not* grant license for any caller/callee signature mismatches when writing C code (unless your C compiler explicitly documents something else).

> Calling this something like "function call ABI", "register ABI", or similar would resolve both of those issues and would have prevented my own confusion when encountering the idiosyncratic Rust usage.

We do sometimes call this "function call ABI compatibility", but that's a mouthful. All uses of ABI in the Rust compiler generally refer to the function call ABI. Does that not match the typical usage of "ABI"? Anyway changing that terminology (which would be a major change affecting many parts of the compiler) would be a separate thread from this issue.

@traviscross 

ABI compatibility means that a fn call with mismatching caller and callee types behaves like a transmute. It only makes sense to declare ABI compatibility if such a transmute can actually be well-defined for a subset of values of the source type.

Also, ABI compatibility must imply equal alignment (which layout compatibility does not require!) or else calls that pass arguments on the stack would not behave correctly.

Maybe "allows transmutes" is not the right definition for "layout compatible", given this point about alignment... but OTOH "same field offsets" is IMO meaningless as e.g. `i32` has no fields so what would it even mean for that to be layout-compatible with `NonZeroI32`? Or `Option<NonNull<T>>` vs `*mut T`?
author: RalfJung

body:
> That's like saying "x86 asm has less UB than Rust". That's both correct and expected. You seem to make the classic mistake of trying to do asm-level reasoning when thinking about a Rust program -- but that's [just not valid](https://www.ralfj.de/blog/2019/07/14/uninit.html).

No, I understand the levels of abstraction here. I'm just saying that things like size and alignment are usually part of what's called "ABI". See the example I gave above: [chapter 2](https://itanium-cxx-abi.github.io/cxx-abi/abi.html#layout) of the Itanium ABI (the usual standard for C++ these days) is about size, alignment, and field offset. The Rust usage is idiosyncratic from that point of view. No big deal, just giving you my feedback as a newcomer.

> All uses of ABI in the Rust compiler generally refer to the function call ABI. Does that not match the typical usage of "ABI"? 

No, I don't think it matches usual usage—it's only a strict subset of the usual meaning. See above.

> Anyway changing that terminology (which would be a major change affecting many parts of the compiler) would be a separate thread from this issue.

Agreed, just making you aware in passing of this difficulty for newcomers.

Other chapters of the Itanium ABI are about function calls though. "ABI compatible" is meant to say that they are treated identically wrt *all* aspects/chapters of the ABI, not just *some* of them.

But, point taken about that being confusing. It's hard to pick a good balance between overly verbose and confusingly terse.
author: RalfJung

body:
> ABI compatibility means that a fn call with mismatching caller and callee types behaves like a transmute. It only makes sense to declare ABI compatibility if such a transmute can actually be well-defined for a subset of values of the source type.

I don't think this is necessarily the case, right? For example given that we *can* split a struct into different registers, you could have struct A and B being ABI compatible while having different layouts (e.g., because there's padding in the struct that doesn't actually get passed when lowering to the underlying ABI). I'm not sure there's any ABIs *currently* used in rustc where we do something like this *and* want to guarantee that externally as an ABI-compatible definition.

One way we could imagine this being useful is that in principle we could define `arg: &[T]` as ABI compatible with `arg1: *const T, arg2: usize`, if we always lowered the first of those into the latter.

(In any case we should probably take this to Zulip or a separate thread).

  %0 = getelementptr inbounds i8, ptr %_1, i64 16
  store i64 0, ptr %0, align 8
  call void @llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64(ptr align 8 %_1, ptr align 8 @anon.099dafc678df7d266c25f95ccf6cde22.0, i64 16, i1 false)
  call void @llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64(ptr align 8 %_0, ptr align 8 %_1, i64 24, i1 false)
  call void @llvm.lifetime.end.p0(i64 24, ptr %_1)
  ret void
}
```

Here's where LLVM's `MemCpyOpt` changes the 16-byte memcpy of undef plus a 8-bytes store into a 24-byte memset: <https://godbolt.org/z/WWvvxhE4n>

body:
Bisected to nightly-2025-11-24 which included #147827, as noted in OP. CI artifacts from they aren't available so couldn't easily bisect further. Also, `-Zmir-enable-passes=-GVN` gives the "good" asm again, which also points to #147827

On the LLVM side, it seems like the `MemCpyOptPass` pass is the main issue; at that point in the opt pipeline, the IR is basically `memcpy(&mut dest.data, const { &MaybeUninit::uninit() }); dest.cap = 0;`, and `MemCpyOptPass` seems to change it into `memset(&mut dest, 0)`: ([godbolt link](https://rust.godbolt.org/z/bGW1Gse8P), see "Opt Pipeline" view)

```llvm
// before MemCpyOptPass pass
@0 = private unnamed_addr constant [16 x i8] undef, align 8

define void @example[9407090cffdc3c0d]::make(ptr dead_on_unwind noalias nofree noundef writable writeonly sret([24 x i8]) align 8 captures(none) dereferenceable(24) %_0) unnamed_addr {
start:
  tail call void @llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64(ptr noundef nonnull align 8 dereferenceable(16) %_0, ptr noundef nonnull align 8 dereferenceable(16) @0, i64 16, i1 false)
  %_1.sroa.4.0._0.sroa_idx = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %_0, i64 16
  store i64 0, ptr %_1.sroa.4.0._0.sroa_idx, align 8
  ret void
}
```

```llvm
// after MemCpyOptPass pass
@0 = private unnamed_addr constant [16 x i8] undef, align 8

define void @example[9407090cffdc3c0d]::make(ptr dead_on_unwind noalias nofree noundef writable writeonly sret([24 x i8]) align 8 captures(none) dereferenceable(24) %_0) unnamed_addr {
start:
  %_1.sroa.4.0._0.sroa_idx = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %_0, i64 16 // this is removed by a later InstCombine pass
  call void @llvm.memset.p0.i64(ptr align 8 %_0, i8 0, i64 24, i1 false)
  ret void
}
```

For comparison, the IR at this stage in the LLVM pipeline with  ` -Zmir-enable-passes=-GVN` (I think):

```llvm
define void @example[9407090cffdc3c0d]::make(ptr dead_on_unwind noalias nofree noundef writable writeonly sret([24 x i8]) align 8 captures(none) dereferenceable(24) %_0) unnamed_addr {
start:
  %_1.sroa.4.0._0.sroa_idx = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %_0, i64 16
  store i64 0, ptr %_1.sroa.4.0._0.sroa_idx, align 8
  ret void
}
```

~~Maybe LLVM treats `constant undef` differently from an uninitialized `alloca`? The unoptimized LLVM IR that rustc emits in the "bad" version has a `@anon.05d519269bd06692ed4427bd5298e9b5.0 = private unnamed_addr constant [16 x i8] undef, align 8` that it `memcpy`s from, whereas the "good" version without `GVN` instead copies from an uninitialized `alloca` ([godbolt link](https://rust.godbolt.org/z/hWjq3hWcq) comparison).~~ edit: see [here](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/157743#issuecomment-4677590026)

body:
I suggest breaking all these registers into separate crates, possibly along arbitrary boundaries, then re-exporting them through a facade crate. If possible, I also suggest removing trait impls or helper functions from the bitflags macro expansion.

It is infeasible for a compiler to have better than O(n) scaling, so it's quite odd that you pointed that out.

There are probably other things we could do to improve this scenario, but to be honest this entire issue is just "rustc is inefficient" and while I agree with you, I think our inefficiency is death by a thousand cuts.

I think there are probably some optimizations we could implement that would improve resource use for this build but it is unlikely to be percentages large enough to be exciting and merged quickly enough to unblock your work. For example, every `1 << 0` is lowered as an inline const and it is just a bit too complicated for my trivial consts optimization to apply: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/148040. It could be extended to consider those trivial. But that's probably a drop in the bucket compared to the dozens of `const fn` bodies that get compiled per register.

body:
update: i opened https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/158362 for this.

the repro still matches this issue. the problem is not that we need to register empty assumptions for every binder path. `eagerly_handle_placeholders` was walking up to the infcx's current universe, even when the current solver region constraint did not mention those universes. that made it call `get_placeholder_assumptions` for unrelated universes and hit the unwrap.

the pr bounds the eager pass by `max_universe` of the current region constraint. imo this is the cleaner fix: if the constraint cannot name a universe, there is nothing useful to eagerly handle for that universe. idk if there is a deeper cleanup to do later, but ltm this keeps the existing assumptions machinery intact instead of making missing entries silently mean ambiguity.

This is the first time I have been pinged for the release notes process. I cannot edit the issue description, but I think that:

* The section should be Compatibility Notes, since this is a bug fix that can never change behavior except by stopping code from compiling.
* The note should not primarily mention `StructuralPartialEq`, because that is an unstable implementation detail of [the rules for matching constants](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/patterns.html?highlight=structural#constant-patterns). Instead, it should say something like:

  > Closed a hole in the pattern matching [structural equality](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/patterns.html#constant-patterns) check, preventing cases where a match of a constant would be allowed, despite disagreeing with a manually written `PartialEq` implementation, when a `derive(PartialEq)` implementation for that type also exists.

>  you should NOT combine backchain and packed-stack (unless combined with softfloat for the kernel) **in the same compilation unit**.

(emphasis mine)

As long as that's a per-compilation-unit requirement, not a global one, the current checks should be fine. No reason to use `-Zllvm-target-feature`.

Though of course if the target maintainers think that `backchain` should only be changed globally, and it should be impossible to use e.g. a `std` without "backchain" together with an application with "backchain", then we should use `-Zllvm-target-feature` (or a separate target *modifier* flag). author: RalfJung

body:
Let me try to summarize again.  This whole issue is a bit tricky as we need to consider the interaction of *three* distinct options: `backchain`, `packed-stack`, and `soft-float`.   The following main principles apply:

- `soft-float` is a global ABI-changing option that affects interoperability.  Either everything or nothing must be built with `soft-float`.  (De facto usage: the Linux kernel uses `soft-float` globally, all user-space code including libraries does *not* use `soft-float`.)
- `backchain` does (generally) not affect interoperability  You can switch between `backchain` and `no-backchain` at any function boundary, either between or within a compilation unit.  *However*, in order to actually use the backchain for stack unwinding for debug purposes, all relevant code must be built with `backchain`.  We consider this a "soft" requirement that's up to the user to ensure if they care about this, the compiler should not enforce anything here.  (De facto usage: code by default does not use backchain, it is only enabled manually in some places that have specific debugging needs, e.g. the Linux kernel or some user-space environments like JITs where some code does not come with proper DWARF CFI.)
- `packed-stack` does not affect interoperability at all, and there is no observable side effect of intermixing packed and non-packed functions whatsoever.  However, it is impossible to generate code using *both* `backchain` *and* `packed-stack`, *unless* `soft-float` is also in effect.  This is a fully local requirement that applies on a per-function basis and must be enforced by the compiler (or else the back-end will abort with an internal error).  (De facto usage: not normally used in user-space.  Always used by the Linux kernel where kernel stack space is precious.  Note that the kernel also uses both `backchain` and `soft-float`, so the requirement is satisfied.)

>  In particular I wonder what happens if some compilation units use -Ctarget-feature=+backchain, some use -Zpacked-stack, but none of them use both so the check does not get triggered.

This works fine.  (With the exception that of course you will not get a reliable backtrace, as always when usage of `backchain` is inconsistent across the whole program.)

body: `backchain` is represented as a target feature, `packed-stack` is a dedicated compiler flag. Is there a specific reason for that difference?
author: RalfJung

body:
> `backchain` is represented as a target feature, `packed-stack` is a dedicated compiler flag. Is there a specific reason for that difference?

Right now, the LLVM back-end does not actually have a `packed-stack` target feature.  Thinking about this more, this seems to be more of an historical accident.   Initially, neither `packed-stack` nor `backchain` were supported as target features.  Rather, both features could only be triggered via LLVM IR *function attributes*.  The `-mbackchain` and `-mpacked-stack` command line arguments to Clang set the corresponding function attribute on all functions of the current compilation unit.

The target feature for `backchain` was introduced much later here: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/71668, with the argument that this is needed to enable the `__attribute__((target("backchain")))` syntax for GCC compatibility.   The same was never done for `packed-stack` - even though the same argument could have been made; GCC does suport `__attribute__((target("packed-stack")))` as well.  I guess the difference is that there is some code out there using the former but not the latter.

Nevertheless, if it would make Rust integration easier, I guess we could just add a `packed-stack` target feature to LLVM with the same reasoning.  This would implicitly add a dependency on a (future) LLVM version to Rust, though.
author: uweigand

body:
I'd like us to first and foremost think about the UI we want to expose from the Rust side. We can have something be a target feature in Rust without it being a target feature in LLVM. (Though that is a bit of a pain. We should probably make it easier to implement that rather than adding ad-hoc hacks each time we need this.)

I am not sure about what the trade-offs are between making something a target feature vs. a `-C` flag. Some differences that come to mind:
- A `-C` flag makes it seem much more "built-in" to the compiler. Every such flag is a dedicated field in the rust compiler session, target specs (if applicable), and so on.
- Target features can typically be enabled (but not disabled!) on a per-function basis (`#[target_feature]`), and can be queried via cfg (`cfg!(target_feature)`).

I don't know how to use those differences to decide what makes most sense for any particular flag, but I noticed you talking about `backchain` and `packed-stack` as very similar kinds of things so it would seem odd that we make a different decision for the two of them.

@rust-lang/compiler if someone has thoughts on target features vs compiler flags, or if we maybe even have some useful precedent or guidelines for that, please chime in. :)

It just occurred to me that if we make `packed-stack` a target-feature we automatically support it via the `#[target_feature]` function attribute. This means one can endup with a call-stack where `backchain` and `packed-stack` is mixed. I doubt that we want to analyze each and every possible call-stack during compilation to check for this.

So for me this results in the question: 
Should we forbid `backchain` and (if we make `packed-stack` a target-feature) also `target-feature` from being set by function attributes within the code?

OK, I now agree the overall best solution would be to:
- make `packed-stack` a target feature, initially only in the Rust front-end
- in parallel, make `packed-stack` a target feature in LLVM
- once Rust has moved up to the appropriate LLVM version, use the back-end feature in Rust

body:
Also note that [swapping the order of the fields](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=ee434160b78c3a392b2ce6d3e68bd5a3) so that we work with `(Never, i32)` instead of `(i32, Never)` has no effect on the behavior.

Assuming that the compiler checks one field at a time in some consistent order (e.g., check the first element of the tuple before checking the second element), this implies that the compiler checks the entire pattern to see if it's consistent with the value. (Where the `_` pattern is considered to be consistent with a place of type `Never`.) If the entire pattern is consistent, then nothing happens. If at least one subpattern is inconsistent with the value, the UB occurs.

(I initially assumed that UB happens as soon as the code tries to match a value of type `Never` with the pattern `_`. This was incorrect.)

author: theemathas

body:
> pattern-matching triggers UB when an irrefutable pattern doesn't match the value.

Correct

> To me, the main oddity is that exhaustive_patterns considers the (123, _) pattern irrefutable

That has a simple explanation: exhaustive_patterns is a relic from a past time when we were more casual with empty types; it's not fit for purpose. That said, I do want to figure out a good story for all this.

We compute refutability by asking "is there a value fir this type that doesn't match this pattern". For ergonomics, the set of values depends on where the data is: I distinguish "safe places" (i.e. not inside a reference, raw ptr or union field) from "unsafe places" (inside a reference, raw ptr or union field). Inside a safe place, empty types have no values; inside an unsafe place, empty types have an Uninit value.

References are unsafe places because it was possible to make a valid `&!`. Now that this seems to be decided against, references can be made safe places. (I know I'm mixing safety and validity, thankfully it doesn't matter anymore). What exhaustive_patterns does is make all places behave like safe places, which is why it's not good.

All that said, it does feel weird to me to ever consider `let (123, _)`/`let (123, !)` irrefutable, but I'm not sure how to make that precise. It can't be just "error if we find a refutable subpattern next to a never subpattern", because that would rule out `(true, !) | (false, !)`. I also can't consider all places unsafe when checking for refutability, as that would rule out `let Ok(_)` on a `Result<T, !>`.
author: Nadrieril

body:
>  it does feel weird to me to ever consider let (123, _)/let (123, !) irrefutable

For `(123, !)` this seems entirely natural to me -- I'd say that `(p, !)` is irrefutable for any pattern `p`.

A pattern is irrefutable if we'd allow it as the sole arm in a `match`, and `(123, !)` qualifies for that, doesn't it?
author: RalfJung

body:
> > How do you deduce this from that example?
> 
> [@RalfJung](https://github.com/RalfJung) `let` statements (without an `else`) [require](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/reference/statements.html#r-statement.let.constraint) an irrefutable pattern for the code to compile.

@theemathas 

No I don't think this is the correct deduction at all. In fact you need no patterns at all since
```
fn foo(x: (i32, Never)) {
    match x {}
}
```
this works.

Given, `match x {}` works, I'm unsurprised that `match { ANY_PATTERN => (…) }` would work for any pattern (of the right type). And then in turn, it's unsurprising that `let ANY_PATTERN = x;` will work. Or what do you think?

---

Edit: On second thought, maybe the question of whether or not to call it "irrefutable" depends on how to define that term "irrefutable". Refutability seems a weird concept in a context where nothing ever matches. You could also call the patter "always refuting" since it's still impossible to match against it; the point is that at the time the pattern matching begins, you already know you'll never reach there.

body: there are differences between no arms, `_ =>` and `binding_pattern =>` with regards to UB, aren't there?  It's unsurprising that the compiler currently allows this, because of what you said, but it probably *shouldn't* because of those differences?

body:
> Given, match x {} works, I'm unsurprised that match { ANY_PATTERN => (…) } would work for any pattern (of the right type). And then in turn, it's unsurprising that let ANY_PATTERN = x; will work. Or what do you think?

That's an incorrect analogy: `match *ptr { _ => {} }` *does not read the pointer* even if `match *ptr {}` compiles. You should think of  `match *ptr {}` as desugaring to something like `match *ptr { ! }`, i.e. a match with an explicit pattern that indicates the act of doing case-distinction on an empty type.

body: `--print target-features` just prints two sets of features: The all target features rust natively supports together with rustc provided descriptions and the target features LLVM supports but don't map to a rust target feature together with the LLVM provided description. soft-float is in the latter category as it is below the "Code-generation features supported by LLVM for this target:" header. `-Ctarget-feature` accepts rust target features, but if rustc doesn't recognize a target feature, it will be passed verbatim to LLVM together with this warning. In any case `rustc +nightly --target mips-unknown-linux-musl --print target-spec-json -Zunstable-options ` shows that `soft-float` is passed to LLVM by default already, so no need to explicitly set it. In any case be aware that enabling soft-float does not prevent all float instructions, merely float computation instructions. The calling convention may still require passing floats in float registers, which requires a register move to a float register. And according to https://techpubs.jurassic.nl/library/manuals/2000/007-2816-004/sgi_html/ch02.html the o32 abi that mips-unknown-linux-musl uses does in fact require passing some float args in float registers.

body:
I'm fairly certain this is an LLVM bug rather than a `rustc` issue. A minimal reproducer in plain IR:

```llvm
; Minimal reproducer: the fixed-width <2 x i64> partial.reduce.add pattern
; that rustc/LoopVectorize emitted for the popcount-sum loop.
target triple = "aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu"

declare <16 x i8> @llvm.ctpop.v16i8(<16 x i8>)
declare <2 x i64> @llvm.vector.partial.reduce.add.v2i64.v16i64(<2 x i64>, <16 x i64>)
declare i64 @llvm.vector.reduce.add.v2i64(<2 x i64>)

define i64 @popcount_sum(ptr %p, i64 %n) {
entry:
  br label %vector.body

vector.body:
  %index = phi i64 [ 0, %entry ], [ %index.next, %vector.body ]
  %acc   = phi <2 x i64> [ zeroinitializer, %entry ], [ %pr, %vector.body ]
  %g     = getelementptr inbounds i8, ptr %p, i64 %index
  %ld    = load <16 x i8>, ptr %g, align 1
  %pc    = call <16 x i8> @llvm.ctpop.v16i8(<16 x i8> %ld)
  %ze    = zext <16 x i8> %pc to <16 x i64>
  %pr    = call <2 x i64> @llvm.vector.partial.reduce.add.v2i64.v16i64(<2 x i64> %acc, <16 x i64> %ze)
  %index.next = add i64 %index, 16
  %done  = icmp eq i64 %index.next, %n
  br i1 %done, label %exit, label %vector.body

exit:
  %r = call i64 @llvm.vector.reduce.add.v2i64(<2 x i64> %pr)
  ret i64 %r
}
```

I have a WIP patch for this behaviour, still iterating through all the cases.

body: Does this miscompile only affect code that uses `as` to turn a boolean into an integer? Or does it affect other code too? Is there a short description of the rough kind of shape of code that might be affected by this miscompilation?
author: theemathas

body:
The faulty optimization isn’t specific to bool-as-int casts. The relevant MIR pattern is:

- A single basic block ending with a branch on a boolean
- The branch condition is a `move` operand rather than a `copy` operand (note that this excludes uses of the comparison result *after*  the branch being optimized)
- That boolean is computed earlier in the same basic block as integer or `char` comparison (SSA local equal/not-equal to a constant)
- That comparison result is also used for any other computation in the same basic block before the branch. Note that this excludes “another branch on the same bool” as that generally means another basic block. Casting to integer is the most likely but not only option here.

It’s hard for me to describe exactly what source code patterns will lead to this MIR. The problematic pass runs very late in the optimization pipeline. Earlier passes may introduce the required ingredients even if they’re not apparent at the source level (e.g., GVN unifying two separate `x == C` expressions). On the other hand, the requirements “`move` operand” and “SSA local” seems to save some simple source code patterns that look like they would be affected.

Rather than trying to guess whether specific code may trigger this miscompilation, I’d suggest updating the compiler or disabling the pass via `-Zmir-passes`.

But the LHS's type is `Duration`. Maybe LHS's type is not being inferred correctly by `suggest_cast`'s caller.

It could be that either this function should be called with `checked_ty = Duration` or should be prevented from being called in the first place, in case this is only called for types which have the `std::convert::From<checked_ty>` trait defined for them ( Since then it makes sense to call `expected_ty::from(checked_ty)` )

- Please correct me if something seems wrong in this.

body:
I think these ***were*** the reproducing instructions

> ### Code
> ```
> ./x setup 
>  - d) dist: Install Rust from source
>  - editor: none
>
> ./x.py build (successful)
> ./x.py test (failed)
> ```

---

This would not be an I-ICE issue though, even though the test output might on a first glance look like it. The actual error is just in the test suite noticing a difference in the error message:

> ```
> The actual stderr differed from the expected stderr
> ```

The ICE is just an intended ICE case in this UI test ; (it's not even a real ICE because it's just a simulated one due to `-Z treat-err-as-bug`).

The mismatch in output is due to the normalization patterns at the start of the file, like 
```rs
//@ normalize-stderr: "note: compiler flags.*\n\n" -> ""
//@ normalize-stderr: "note: rustc.*running on.*" -> "note: rustc {version} running on {platform}"
//@ normalize-stderr: "thread.*panicked at compiler.*" -> ""
//@ normalize-stderr: " +\d{1,}: .*\n" -> ""
//@ normalize-stderr: " + at .*\n" -> ""
//@ normalize-stderr: ".*note: Some details are omitted.*\n" -> ""
```
not being able to handle the change in output for a compiler built for distribution; if I run the test with some stage1 I happen to have ready locally, the stack trace looks like 

```
thread 'rustc' (10628) panicked at compiler/rustc_errors/src/lib.rs:1529:17:
aborting due to `-Z treat-err-as-bug=1`
stack backtrace:
   0: __rustc::rust_begin_unwind
             at /rustc/0417c25868d6dfbd1c291dfeae950504faa6f790/library/std/src/panicking.rs:689:5
   1: core::panicking::panic_fmt
             at /rustc/0417c25868d6dfbd1c291dfeae950504faa6f790/library/core/src/panicking.rs:80:14
[…]
```

whereas with some randmo `nightly` I have, it looks like 
```
thread 'rustc' (10478) panicked at /rustc-dev/362211dc29abc4e8f8cfc384740237f144929b03/compiler/rustc_errors/src/lib.rs:1485:17:
aborting due to `-Z treat-err-as-bug=1`
stack backtrace:
   0:     0x7c8cee17c25b - <<std[3d889afb86ce2054]::sys::backtrace::BacktraceLock>::print::DisplayBacktrace as core[a21a857a14d05de]::fmt::Display>::fmt
   1:     0x7c8cee82ed08 - core[a21a857a14d05de]::fmt::write
[…]
```

The normalization of

```rs
//@ normalize-stderr: "thread.*panicked at compiler.*" -> ""
```
in particular doesn't match the output of my nightly compiler, as that has the extra `/rustc-dev/…HASH_VALUE…` kind of prefix.

Hence I believe by doing `x setup` for profile `dist`, the reported behavior happens in the same manner. (I don't want to recompile my rustc in `dist` at the moment to try out.)

---

A possible fix could be to somehow *deny* `x test` in the `dist` profile altogether, with a nicer error message that just tells you that it isn't supposed to work.

author: workingjubilee

body:
> ```
> ./configure --enable-profiler
> x test
> ```
> 
> Oh that's... interesting. Odd, even. How is that related? I'm almost more concerned that that matters!
> 
> Since we seem to use the more-resilient normalization pattern in other cases, though, reusing it seems like it should be fine.

I checked again and it's a bit less interesting than it seems. The config generated by configure defaults to the dist profile 😄

It's actually `rust.remap-debuginfo = true` from the dist profile that triggers this, and a clean build directory is needed too. `run.sh` forces it off for non-DEPLOY builds which is why the regular test jobs don't fail, but our internal CI doesn't invoke run.sh and so picked it up.

body:
> However, at the same time, I've found a strange issue. In the updated test, #[export_stable = 1] not only reports the malformed attribute input error but also private items not exportable. This indicates that even if the attribute parameter is malformed, fn test is still being loaded with AttributeKind::ExportStable? This is odd; is there something I haven't considered?

This is deliberate, if arguments are provided to an attribute that does not expect arguments we remove the arguments and continue in the compilation, so we can generate more errors. I think this situation is fine here was well, since the two errors are two separate problems

> Is #[export_stable] even supposed to exist outside of the generated sdylib interface files?

I'm also not sure, cc @m-ou-se
author: JonathanBrouwer

body:
> Is `#[export_stable]` even supposed to exist outside of the generated sdylib interface files?

My current implementation takes the issue literally (run validation on all crate types, so `bin` gets the same 16 errors as `sdylib`). If the answer is instead "the attribute shouldn't exist outside sdylib", the fix would be to reject `#[export_stable]` outright on non-sdylib crates (different errors).

body: From what I can tell, [the pass's logic for shuffling StorageDeads around](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/d29dae8d17abb191a24f57eb00f68ebc1b168314/compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/simplify_comparison_integral.rs#L107) tries to identify StorageDeads that would interfere with extending the lifetime of the comparison result, and *sink* them into successor blocks (i.e., after the `switchInt`). In this case, the block is its own successor, so the StorageDead gets *hoisted* unintentionally. Presumably this problem can occur for any block involved in a loop.

I think what happens is that rustdoc failed to parse the test code as function body and then simply skipped wrapping the doctest in a function, thus asking rustc to literally parse

```rust

x.push_mut("bar");

as module, for which this is a totally reasonable error message, rather than


```rust
#[test]
fn foo() {

x.push_mut("foo")
x.push_mut("bar");
}
```

as would normally be the case if there was no syntax error.

Yes, `unsafe` is obviously necessary when the `target_feature` value isn't available for the whole compilation.

body: I think clang uses the sysv abi on UEFI unless explicitly told otherwise as required for GNU-EFI, while rustc follows the MSVC ABI on UEFI as required for EDK2. In other words the problem is that you are effectively compiling your Rust and C code for a fundamentally different target. Try compiling your C code with clang-cl instead for a Windows target.
author: bjorn3

body:
@bjorn3 I tested it again with clang-cl, but the result was the same.

The target was set to x86_64-unknown-uefi.
The x86_64-unknown-uefi target uses the Windows ABI.

In fact, the current issue is that the calling convention for u128 is different, but the argument order (rcx, rdx, r8, r9) is identical.
Aside from u128, there were absolutely no issues with other parts.

In rust, it is called as `__udivti3(u128*, u128*)`, and in clang, it is called as `__udivti3(u64 lo, u64 hi, u64 lo, u64 hi)`.
author: jclab-joseph

body: For me `clang --target=x86_64-pc-windows` will call it as `__udivti3(u128*, u128*)`  just like rustc while `clang --target=x86_64-unknown-uefi` will call it as `__udivti3(u64 lo, u64 hi, u64 lo, u64 hi)`: https://rust.godbolt.org/z/dKs7YT7c6 The former is the most consistent ABI. I'm not saying it is the correct one as MSVC doesn't support `uint128_t` in the first place and thus Microsoft hasn't specified any ABI for it yet.
author: bjorn3

body:
rust.godbolt.org is a great site!

It feels strange that there is no consistency with clang targets only in rust. doesn't Rust also use LLVM internally?

It might be related to https://github.com/rust-lang/compiler-builtins/pull/475.
(However, win64_128bit_abi_hack is now gone)
author: jclab-joseph

body:
> doesn't Rust also use LLVM internally?

Yes. The reason the calling convention doesn't always match is that half of the calling convention code mapping high level types to units that can be passed in registers have to be reproduced in every frontend as LLVM IR doesn't have a rich enough type system to represent all C types in a lossless way as necessary for determining the exact lowering of argument types to registers. In addition rustc uses x86_64-unknown-windows as LLVM target for x86_64-unknown-uefi: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/4429659e4745016bd3f26a4a421843edc7fbc422/compiler/rustc_target/src/spec/targets/x86_64_unknown_uefi.rs#L33 There was no dedicated x86_64-unknown-uefi target in LLVM back when support for it was added to rustc.

author: ChrisDenton

body:
I haven't seen this in practice, so no, I'm not exactly sure whether this is real.

> It mentions that it's the number of "ticks" since boot, it's only a signed number for the sake of calculations and it will never be 0 (if it were able to be negative then it would be likely to hit zero at some point unless it was fudged somehow).

The return value of `QueryPerformanceCounter` is never zero (which would indicate failure), but it doesn't say that the returned tick count is never zero – at least I understand it that way and that would match the documentation on [QueryPerformanceCounter](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/profileapi/nf-profileapi-queryperformancecounter) which documents the non-zero guarantee for the return value:
> If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
>
> If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call [GetLastError](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/desktop/api/errhandlingapi/nf-errhandlingapi-getlasterror). On systems that run Windows XP or later, the function will always succeed when given valid parameters and will thus never return zero.

The forum discussion I linked in the issue description provides at least [anecdotal evidence for negative tick counts](https://www.pouet.net/topic.php?which=12684&page=1#c589706):
> My teammates have been using this same code for ~10 years and the common consensus amongst them is that it is surprising, but normal, to get very negative (like -318596), but increasing, timestamps from QPC.

While I should note that this evidence is later [questioned](https://www.pouet.net/topic.php?which=12684&page=1#c589709) by other posters, I think given the negligible cost of `div_euclid`/`rem_euclid` over unsigned division that it makes sense to correctly handle negative tick counts, even though I agree that one can infer from the documentation that they should not occur.

body:
Someone I talked to suggested this idea: While checking whether a pattern matches a type, we allow the compiler to reorder accesses to the scrutinee however it wants, with the exception of union patterns. For union patterns, everything outside any union patterns must be checked before the compiler is allowed to check anything inside a union pattern.

To be precise, we define dependencies between the subpatterns in a pattern. Subpattern X depends on subpattern Y if [the set of union patterns that X is in] is a strict superset of [the set of union patterns that Y is in]. (We also have the preexisting dependency where everything inside an enum pattern depends on the enum discriminant check.) The compiler is required to check all of a subpattern's dependencies before checking that subpattern.

I think that this would allow maximal flexibility to the compiler, without causing surprises to users. Union patterns are singled out due to being the only kind of pattern that requires unsafe access to stuff. Any other way of trying to observe the ordering of subpattern evaluation, I believe, requires a scrutinee whose safety requirements are broken.

Edit: lol, ninja'd by Nadrieril proposing a similar (but not identical) idea above.

#156027 doesn't fix this (but it's certainly touches the same code!). This should be *fairly* trivial to fix. It's not actually the `item_bounds` call that's relevant, but rather the param_env bounds; the idea is that we need to "elaborate" the param_env:

The alias ty visited by `FreeRegionsVisitor` is not `T:BarAssoc`, it's `<<T as Bar>::BarAssoc as Foo>::FooAssoc<'_>`. So, I guess you're saying that we shouldn't be looking at the `T: Bar` in the param env, but rather recursing through to `<T as Bar>::BarAssoc`? Sure, that would work with the code as-written today, but doesn't work with how this has been refactored in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/156027/changes#diff-5d86c3fc35a603e984030459eb67d4870a975e53a460c331f15e48813ce8ce0eR27.

I think the point still remains that whether or not you elaborate bounds starting from the param env or if you start from the `Self` type of the alias, the underlying point I'm trying to make is that this is effectively an "extension" of the `param_env.caller_bounds()`. Once #156027 lands, this still fairly easy to do: you would add another loop through the additional bounds from the self type, like we do for the `param_env.caller bounds()`: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/156027/changes#diff-5d86c3fc35a603e984030459eb67d4870a975e53a460c331f15e48813ce8ce0eR546

> Just spit-balling, but since `ErrorKind` is (unstable) in `core::io` now, maybe `libc` could provide mappings for the POSIX platforms instead? Currently, `std` _mostly_ defers to `libc` for the POSIX platforms but still has a few platform specific changes. Yeah, that's a tidy option. Since ErrorKind's already in core, libc could reference it under rustc-dep-of-std today.

What I keep coming back to is that it only moves the POSIX half: windows, uefi and the rest still decode in std, so the decode ends up split across two repos. Sitting next to the constants is the real upside, but landing half of it in a separately-pinned crate is the cost against it

The way I see the options:
1. Add the missing arms to the copies as they are. Smallest, but they can drift again.
 2. One shared POSIX decode in std, each target adding only its deltas. Keeps it in one place and stops the drift, no cross-repo part.
3. The libc version. Closest coupling between an errno and its kind, but the biggest change and the most tied to where the core::io move ends up.

To summarize our current findings from that discussion thread:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/158067 was the PR that introduced the sporadic failures

cc @TimNN @dianqk

The issue is probably due to randomize-layout in the codegen-llvm suite.

The test was made more imprecise in a way that is probably unnecessary, while being made more precise in ways that are brittle in the face of randomize-layout.

The line
```
    // CHECK: [[INNER:%.*]] = load ptr, ptr %x
```
is not resilient to the load sometimes being from `%x` and sometimes being from a pointer assigned to `%0` that is itself GEP'd from `%x`

body:
They do have dedicated opcodes, actually! That's sort of The Actual Problem. The various FPUs (since x86-64 is cursed to have 2...) were gradual additions on a basis of a comparatively "simple" set of integer registers (first 8, then 16, probably soon 32...) and the entire reason for x86-64 instead of Itanium was backward compatibility, and it has instructions like `XSAVE` which are designed to quickly save "all extended processor state"... useful for shenanigans like quickly saving a thread's state, or even actually doing FPU operations in kernel mode[^0]! The exact amount of FPU state the CPU can have could vary, so the kernel executing on the hardware may only be aware of and manage space for less extended state than the CPU actually has, so the CPU will "play dumb" and pretend less state is active or treat vector instructions as illegal instructions until the OS explicitly okays things.

And obviously you can also just, as a bare-metal program, simply turn them on and go to town if you have no userspace programs to worry about. It's just setting a bit in a magic register.

This process is mostly described in Volume 3 of the [Intel Software Developer's Manual](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/content-details/922475/intel-64-and-ia-32-architectures-software-developer-s-manual-combined-volumes-1-2a-2b-2c-2d-3a-3b-3c-3d-and-4.html), "System Programming Guide", with 12.2 x87 FPU Initialization and 12.6 Initializing SSE/SSE2/SSE3/SSSE. (Exact number of the chapter may vary based on version.)

[^0]: OS kernels often only save the integer registers on context-switch. They get away with only saving that much because they don't use the rest.

The original issue report:
> On stable in debug mode, it works as expected at 1GB and 2GB, but the 4GB version prints a random different value every time (not 123). This seems likely to be a soundness issue, so I'm labeling this I-unsound.

The purpose of the test is to work with a 4GB stack in order to verify an issue does not recur, so we need some "slack" around the 4GB in order for running the test to make sense. So we cannot reduce the size of the requested memory below, say, 4.1GB, and at that point we might as well ask for the 5th GB since we've already "broken the bank" for anything with only 4GB RAM.

author: Manishearth

body:
The safety issue here is indirect.There may be a problem if you pass a reference to a struct that contains pointers that may be dereferenced by the kernel. This doesn't affect most values since they're usually integers or handles but it does affect some.

So I'd agree that either this or `spawn_with_attributes` should be unsafe.
author: ChrisDenton

body:
Indeed.

I think in a way it would make a bit more sense to put the `unsafe` on `spawn_with_attributes` because that's most probably where the UB could really happen as the API used by `ProcThreadAttributeListBuilder` is most probably safe when used strictly by itself, although still undocumented. It would also maintain the intention of having a "safe" wrapper around the (more) unsafe `raw_attribute`.

However, putting it on `attribute` could be safer in practice as it would gate all current and future uses of `ProcThreadAttributeList`. It would also make the unsafety more clearly about the list rather than the rest of the spawn. If I'm not mistaken, I think I've already seen this scheme used in a few places of the standard library, where the indirect safety is still put on the originating constructor even though its operation is not unsafe purely on its own, but most uses of it would be.

Getting rid of all unsafe markers may require modelling all value types with safe equivalents, which could prove to be more work than necessary when in the end we don't have documented safety requirements anyway.
author: PaulDance

body: From the point of an unsafe reviewer, I'm always happier to see safety obligations that are dischargeable/proveable _nearby_. So having `attribute` be unsafe is better. But I can see other reasons to go the other way, and I presume this API is called with the actual set call right next to builder stuff so it's probably not a big deal either way.
author: Manishearth

body:
The (potentially) unsound API is `spawn_with_attributes`. For `ProcThreadAttributeList` to be the one to uphold the safety obligations at a minium we need to document that the memory referenced by any pointers in values live at least as long as the `ProcThreadAttributeList` (and are also otherwise valid for the attribute).

It's also somewhat concerning the `ProcThreadAttributeList` is (by design) extensible so additional attributes may be added in the future. Those attributes could potentially change the way `CreateProcess` works so we can't document with 100% certainty what the safety obligations are for every future option. So I do believe the note to consult the Microsoft documentation is warranted.
author: ChrisDenton

body:
> For ProcThreadAttributeList to be the one to uphold the safety obligations at a minium we need to document that the memory referenced by any pointers in values live at least as long as the ProcThreadAttributeList 

I believe the lifetimes should cover that already, but I'm not sure.

"Valid for the attribute" is the part I think needs to be mentioned (and we need to spend time figuring out what that means)
author: Manishearth

body:
> I believe the lifetimes should cover that already, but I'm not sure.

I don't quite think it does. To take a concrete example, see [`UMS_CREATE_THREAD_ATTRIBUTES`](https://docs.rs/windows-sys/latest/windows_sys/Win32/System/SystemServices/struct.UMS_CREATE_THREAD_ATTRIBUTES.html):

```rust
#[repr(C)]
pub struct UMS_CREATE_THREAD_ATTRIBUTES {
    pub UmsVersion: u32,
    pub UmsContext: *mut c_void,
    pub UmsCompletionList: *mut c_void,
}
```

We can, via a reference, enforce the lifetime of the struct itself but there's no way to enforce the lifetime of the pointers it contains. The ideal solution here is that `UMS_CREATE_THREAD_ATTRIBUTES` is wrapped in something that does capture lifetimes but the `attribute` method can't enforce that.

body:
This is a known issue with function pointers, because a DefId is needed to apply user-supplied generic types, but during type checking function pointers don't have an accessible DefId.

There might be another way to get a DefId, or to apply user-supplied generics, I'm not sure.

Also, if if there aren't any user-supplied types to apply, we could just use inference, and succeed here instead of an ICE.

More details in this thread:
https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/427678-t-lang.2Finterop/topic/Splat.20testing/near/606873232

There's also a UI test for the ICE (without generics) here:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/main/tests/ui/splat/splat-fn-ptr-tuple.rs

Edit:
Next steps:
- if there aren't any user-supplied generics to apply, stop requiring a DefId
- add the regression test for user-supplied fn ptr generics from [this Zulip message](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/427678-t-lang.2Finterop/topic/Splat.20testing/near/606834713)
